item.title: [MLB.com] Dodgers tab Skubal for Game 1 of NLCS, then Yamamoto in Game 2

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers' elite starting pitching was the driving force when they successfully defended their World Series title in 2025. As the back-to-back champions bid for a three-peat, their four-headed monster of a rotation has already been just as impactful four games into their postseason.
Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow recorded a combined 1.69 ERA (four earned runs in 21 1/3 innings) in four games in the NL Division Series against the Braves, the second-lowest mark among this year's postseason rotations. The Rays' starters hold a slight edge with a 1.65 ERA (three earned runs in 16 1/3 innings) in three games.
"To see it play out in the way it did was not surprising," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said. "But just the way they went out and competed, the way they challenged each other, we're excited for this next round and for them to get us deep into games and be a huge part of us, hopefully, winning eight more games."
As the second seed in the NL field, the Dodgers had a bye week and were able to reset their rotation to their liking for the postseason. Because they won the NLDS in four games, they'll be able to tweak their starting four again ahead of their NL Championship Series against the Brewers, which begins on Sunday at American Family Field.
With manager Dave Roberts announcing on Friday that Skubal will start Game 1 and Yamamoto Game 2, here's how the Dodgers' rotation could look through the first four games:
Skubal would have started a winner-take-all Game 5 against the Braves on Friday, but the Dodgers took care of business in four. So they'll send their big Trade Deadline reinforcement to the hill for the NLCS opener against the Brewers, who were among the other teams interested in acquiring him this summer.
Milwaukee also has yet to officially announce its rotation order, but Jacob Misiorowski appears lined up to start opposite Skubal, setting up a must-see matchup between the back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner and this year's presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner.
The Dodgers raised eyebrows by waiting until Game 3 to start Yamamoto in the NLDS. They actually made that decision with the NLCS in mind, as Yamamoto will likely jump ahead of Snell to start Game 2 on his usual five days' rest. Yamamoto would then be available to start a potential Game 6 on his normal rest as well.
Yamamoto has never started on fewer than five days' rest with the Dodgers, but he won last year's World Series MVP honors after closing out Game 7 on zero days' rest. The right-hander said he would be open to pitching on shorter rest and/or in relief again this postseason, but L.A. will try to keep him working on his typical rest unless the situation necessitates it.
Snell showed some rust when he started NLDS Game 2, which was just his third appearance in the span of 2 1/2 weeks because of left groin tightness that flared up in mid-September. He would be working on extended rest if the Dodgers push him to Game 3, but having some more time to fine-tune his delivery might be helpful given how little he has pitched recently.
Remarkably, the Dodgers are 7-0 when Glasnow pitches in a postseason game for them. That Glasnow is the No. 4 starter in this rotation speaks to the depth of the group, as he could be the ace on many other staffs around the Majors.

item.title: [MLB.com] All signs pointing to a dream Skubal-Miz showdown for NLCS Game 1
item.dc:creator: Max Ralph

item.content:encoded:
You get what’s shaping up to be pretty much the best pitching matchup you could ask for in Game 1 of the NL Championship Series.
The Dodgers announced Friday that Tarik Skubal will get the ball in Game 1 on Sunday, and while the Brewers haven't made anything official, they are in prime position to have ace Jacob Misiorowski on the mound. Both teams clinched their spot in the NLCS on Thursday, the Brewers with a 3-1 win over the Padres and the Dodgers with a 4-1 win over the Braves.
Misiorowski pitched just once in the series, throwing four innings of two-run ball in Game 1. Similarly, Skubal opened things against the Braves, going six innings with just one run allowed, and did not pitch again. Both should be well-rested.
The most realistic argument against a Skubal-Misiorowski duel lies in October superstar Yoshinobu Yamamoto, but the Dodgers righty pitched in Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday, meaning he’d start Sunday on just four days’ rest. He will pitch in Game 2 on Monday with a regular recovery that would make more sense.
We’ve seen great pitching in the 2026 postseason thus far and several marquee matchups: Cam Schlittler vs. Payton Tolle; Chris Sale vs. Jesús Luzardo; Max Fried vs. Sonny Gray; Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen; Yamamoto vs. Sale.
If it happens, Skubal vs. Misiorowski will take the cake.
After some struggles late in the regular season, Misiorowski pitched behind an opener when he made his postseason debut a year ago, but he was effective in three appearances. He allowed only one run across seven innings in the NLDS against the Cubs, before striking out nine and yielding just one run in five innings against the Dodgers in the NLCS.
But this is not the same Miz in 2026. The flame-throwing 24-year-old finished the regular season with MLB bests in ERA (1.80), strikeouts (252), WHIP (0.80) and opponents’ batting average (.157). It was more than a breakout -- it was among the greatest pitching seasons in MLB history.
Misiorowski’s four-seam fastball topped out at 104.8 mph and averaged 101.2 mph against the Padres in the NLDS. With the adrenaline that is sure to be present on Sunday, who knows what eye-popping numbers he could put up.
As for Skubal, he won’t win a third consecutive Cy Young. But that won’t take away from the 2.72 ERA he posted in 26 starts, including a 2.61 mark after his blockbuster trade to the Dodgers. Remember, too, that Skubal missed 44 days in the summer after he needed surgery to remove loose bodies in his left elbow. There have been few signs of rust from that recovery.
Skubal’s strong playoff debut with the Dodgers was just more of what we’re used to from the southpaw. He made six postseason starts as a Tiger in 2024 and 2025 with a 2.04 ERA, never going shorter than six innings and allowing more than two runs just once.
The Brewers and Dodgers will already provide appointment viewing throughout the NLCS, a rematch of the 2025 NL pennant battle and a meeting of MLB’s top regular-season teams in 2026. Add in the potential bout of Misiorowski and Skubal in Game 1, and this series should get off to an awfully hot start.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Tarik Skubal starts for Dodgers in NLCS Game 1, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2

Tarik Skubal gets the ball in Game 1 of the National League Championship Series against the Brewers, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 to cover the first two games of the series in Milwaukee, manager Dave Roberts said via Zoom on Friday. item.content:encoded:
Winning the National League Division Series in four games afforded the Dodgers the luxury of setting their starting rotation exactly the way they wanted for the next round. Tarik Skubal gets the ball in Game 1 of the National League Championship Series against the Brewers, with Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 to cover the first two games of the series in Milwaukee, manager Dave Roberts said via Zoom on Friday.
Skubal struck out seven in six innings in his win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 1 of the NLDS. This will be the fourth Game 1 start for Skubal, who has a 1.97 ERA in seven career postseason starts, with 63 strikeouts and seven unintentional walks in 45 2/3 innings, and he's lasted at least six innings in all seven starts.
Yamamoto added to his legend in Game 7 of last year's World Series, getting the final eight outs of Game 7 one day after starting and pitching six innings in Game 6. He's the only pitcher in postseason history to win five straight road appearances while allowing no more than one run in each game, a streak that began in Game 2 of last year's NLCS, also in Milwaukee.
Ahead of his NLDS start, Yamamoto expressed willingness to start on short rest or pitch of out of the bullpen if needed when asked.
"I'm going to get myself ready for any situation. If they want me to go out, then I go out," Yamamoto said, with interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda. "But for me, just those are key things for me. Postseason is just focusing on the game right in front of me."
But this far, every one of Yamamoto's 86 MLB starts — including 10 in the postseason — have come with at least five days rest, and Game 2 comes with five days rest after his 10 strikeouts in seven innings on Tuesday in Atlanta. And starting Yamamoto in Game 2 of a best-of-7 series would allow him to also start in Game 6 on five days rest, while Games 1 and 3 starters would start in Games 5 and 7 on four days rest.
"It's more looking at how he's gotten his rest this year, and what gives him the best chance to pitch potentially two games, Games 2 and 6," Roberts said. "With the off days and the game schedule, that's probably the best way to manage it."

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the calculus the Red Sox have to make when considering a potential contract extension for All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. Be sure to join out FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
Aside from the back-to-back World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers landing back-to-back American League Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal, the Boston Red Sox made the biggest splash at the trade deadline, landing three-time All-Star catcher Adley Rutschman. With only one season of team control remaining, should the Red Sox extend the 28-year-old backstop?
It took a massive haul of prospects to acquire Rutschman from the division rival Baltimore Orioles, including pitchers Anthony Eyanson and Kyson Witherspoon, outfielders Enddy Azocar and Harold Rivas, and Carlos Narvaez, Boston's former starting catcher. After being ranked as a top-10 farm system in the sport ahead of the deadline, the Red Sox saw their farm system fall into the bottom 10 as a result of the trade.
Rutschman was a mixed bag in his first two months in a Red Sox uniform, battling both wrist and elbow issues that saw him in and out of the lineup. After hitting just .187/.253/.363/.615 in his first 25 games in Boston, he ended the regular season hitting .333/.355/.567/.922 in the final seven games.
In 32 regular season games, the 28-year-old hit .222/.278/.410/.688 for Boston. Despite the rough numbers, he was one of the few Red Sox players to get a hit during the team's Wild Card series loss to the New York Yankees, going 1-for-8. Given the cost of acquisition, it's safe to say it was an underwhelming outcome for him at the plate.
However, he was incredibly impressive defensively, particularly with the ABS challenge system. In 34 challenges, Rutschman went 24-10, a 71 percent success rate. Every other Boston catcher went a combined 73-48, good for a 60 percent success rate. Rutschman was a noticeable upgrade over Narvaez, who went 32-27, a 54 percent success rate.
While Rutschman was a mixed bag, the prospect haul it took to acquire him all took off after joining their new organization. For Eyanson and Azocar, it was a continuation of breakout seasons that began in Boston. For Witherspoon, it was his first taste of success in professional baseball after struggling in Boston.
Eyanson, the No. 45-rated prospect in baseball, per MLB Pipeline, posted a 2.03 ERA in six starts with Baltimore's Double-A affiliate Chesapeake. He finished the season with a 1.82 ERA over 79 innings across two levels en route to being named a finalist for the Minor League Pitcher of the Year Award, which went to his former LSU teammate, Seattle Mariners starter Kade Anderson.
After hitting .286/.341/.550/.891 with 18 home runs and 27 doubles while driving in 63 runs, while playing excellent outfield defense in 85 games with Single-A Salem and High-A Greenville, Azocar was one of the biggest risers in the Red Sox system in 2026. His breakout season continued in Baltimore, where he hit .327/.372/.529/.901 with three home runs and eight doubles in 25 games for High-A Frederick. After a breakout season, Azocar now ranks No. 99 in MLB Pipeline's top 100 prospects.
It was a rocky first professional season for Witherspoon, the Red Sox first-round selection in the 2025 MLB Draft. The 21-year-old posted a 4.78 ERA in 17 starts with Greenville before being dealt to Baltimore. However, whatever changes the Orioles made seemed to click, as he allowed only two earned runs in his final three starts.
While Rutschman's numbers in his first two months in Boston don't necessarily warrant a long-term extension, giving up such a substantial prospect package to acquire him puts the Red Sox in a bit of a corner.
If the team waits until next season to see how he performs, they risk him not being interested in signing a deal and instead waiting for free agency, where multiple suitors will assuredly be interested. However, he's likely to command a sizable deal even before hitting the open market, one that, at least based on his time in Boston, he hasn't totally earned.
Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow was asked about potential extension talks between the two sides in Monday's end-of-season press conference, but he offered a nonanswer and instead praised him for his work with the pitching staff.
"Adley stepped in as our primary catcher in the middle of the season, which is not easy to do, especially when pitching is a strength of our team, and immediately endeared himself to the pitching staff, to the coaching staff, to the clubhouse, just a really, really high-quality teammate and leader," Breslow said. "I think that's something we'll develop internally, and any conversations about what Adley's future will look like will take place between Adley's representatives, Adley, and me," he said about a potential extension.
It'll be an interesting calculus for Breslow to make; the initial deal to acquire Rutschman appears to be a mistake after he underperformed and you once again failed to make a deep playoff run. However, a contract extension could compound that mistake, locking in a player who has failed to stay healthy and underperformed in each of the last two seasons.

item.content:encoded:
By splitting the first two games of the National League Division Series, Atlanta essentially turned a five-game series into a three-game series -- and, oh, by the way, stole home-field advantage from the Dodgers in the process.
Next up, each team will turn to its respective staff ace in a pivotal Game 3 as the series shifts to Truist Park on Tuesday night.
“We know it's two good teams going at it,” Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman said. “We know what's at stake on Tuesday. We need to get that win.”
Just how badly does each team need that win? Consider this: In postseason history, the Game 3 winner in a best-of-five series tied 1-1 has gone on to win the series 48 of 67 times (71.6%).
Here’s everything you need to know ahead of the crucial Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 is set for 6 p.m. ET/3 p.m. PT on Tuesday at Truist Park. It will be broadcast on FS1/FOX Deportes/FOX One.
All series are available in the US on MLB.TV with authentication to a participating Pay TV provider. Games are also available live internationally, although not in Canada. Sportsnet is MLB's exclusive English-language broadcaster in Canada for every Postseason game, while TVA Sports will be covering the entire AL Postseason and the World Series in French and Broadcaster RDS will cover the entire NL Postseason in French.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Dodgers: RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto   
Key stat: 0.87 WHIP, ranked second among qualified MLB starters
The reigning World Series MVP is set for his 2026 postseason debut with his team looking to reclaim its series lead. Yamamoto could have started Game 1, but the Dodgers liked the way they were lined up for the NLDS and beyond with Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell starting the first two contests. L.A.'s ace is up third as the series shifts to Atlanta, where he gave up one run across 6 1/3 strong innings on Aug. 27; he was outdueled by Sale in a 1-0 loss.
Braves: LHP Chris Sale   
Key stat:  1.96 ERA over his final 24 regular-season starts
Sale will face the Dodgers for the first time since throwing a five-hit shutout against them on Aug. 27. The 37-year-old posted MLB’s third-best ERA (2.16) this year. He began the postseason by limiting the Phillies to three runs over 6 1/3 innings in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series. There was some thought about having him start Game 2, but because he recorded the final four outs of Game 3 of the WC Series, the Braves pushed him back.
What are the starting lineups?
Dodgers: The big change for LA's Game 3 lineup is Shohei Ohtani in the No. 5 spot. Until Tuesday, Ohtani, recovering from right biceps and left knee injuries, had not been fifth or lower in a starting lineup since Sept. 23, 2020. With Sale on the mound, the Dodgers are not only stacking the top half of their lineup mostly with right-handed hitters, they're shaking up their typical starting nine. They already started Miguel Rojas at third base over Max Muncy when facing a lefty opener in Game 2, so it's not a surprise to see Kiké Hernández getting his first start this postseason at the hot corner, shifting Rojas to second.
Braves: Drake Baldwin’s leadoff homer accounted for the game’s only run the last time the Braves faced Yamamoto. Baldwin, Matt Olson and Michael Harris II should all enjoy seeing a right-handed starter. The Braves had faced a lefty starter in four of their first five postseason games. Aaron Nola, the only right-hander they’ve seen, lasted just 1 2/3 innings in Game 3 of the NLWC Series.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Braves: Coming off an off-day, the Braves will have closer Raisel Iglesias and two top setup men, Robert Suarez and Dylan Lee, available. Didier Fuentes and Ray Kerr won’t be available after both threw 40-plus pitches on Sunday.
Dodgers: The bullpen had to cover the final 5 1/3 innings of Game 2 after a shaky start from Snell, but after a series off-day, the Dodgers should have almost everyone available for Game 3. The exception may be Roki Sasaki, who threw two innings on 36 pitches on Sunday.
Any injuries of note?
Dodgers: Ohtani (right biceps, left knee) and Freeman (right knee) are managing lingering injuries. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option. Blake Treinen (right shoulder inflammation) is unlikely to pitch this postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Braves: Harris has two three-hit efforts in five games this postseason and is 8-for-20 (.400) overall. The Braves hope to get Acuña (3-for-18 without an extra-base hit) and Olson (3-for-19 with seven strikeouts) going as the series goes on.
Dodgers: After a tough September, Freeman (3-for-7, home run) swung the bat well in the first two games. Pages (0-for-7) and Tommy Edman (0-for-5) are seeking their first hits this postseason.
Anything else fans might want to know?
- This will be the first time Sale has faced the Dodgers in the postseason since coming out of the Red Sox bullpen to pitch a perfect ninth inning to conclude the 2018 World Series.
- Roberts enters Game 3 one win shy of 71 managerial postseason wins, which would tie Tony La Russa for second-most all-time. Joe Torre holds the record with 84.

item.content:encoded:
The scenes shift for Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday, Oct. 6, and prediction markets offer great trading opportunities.
Unpredictable things happen during the MLB postseason, but if you think you know what will happen, you can stake your claim on Kalshi and Polymarket US.
Aces Chris Sale and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will square off at Atlanta’s Truist Park in a star-studded pitching matchup between the Braves and two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers. The series is even at 1 after Atlanta’s 3-2 win at Dodger Stadium in Game 2.
The Milwaukee Brewers will try to sweep the San Diego Padres in the nightcap at San Diego’s Petco Park.
Let’s look closer at the best sports prediction markets and prices for today’s two games.
Best MLB props for National League Playoffs today
LA Dodgers at Atlanta Braves over/under market
Why Over 6.5 runs could hit
Probability: 51% at Kalshi
Sale and Yamamoto are aces, but these are two of baseball’s most prolific offenses. The Dodgers, of course, have MVPs batting Nos. 1-3 (Mookie Betts, Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman), and Freeman is heating up after an ice-cold September.
Seven runs isn’t a high bar to clear, especially considering Sale’s struggles in October. Sale has a 5.83 ERA in 12 career postseason appearances and allowed three runs to the Phillies in his last postseason start.
The teams totaled eight runs in Game 1, which Dodgers star Tarik Skubal started.
Why Under 6.5 runs could hit
Probability: 49% at ProphetX
These are two of the best pitchers in baseball, and Yamamoto specifically has been a big-game pitcher since he came over from Japan. He was the 2025 World Series MVP. Fewer than seven runs were scored in five of his nine career postseason starts.
Sale has been a bulldog throughout his career, and he’ll need to rise to the occasion to match Yamamoto in an enormous game.
Even though these offenses have elite players, they have not gotten unlocked. Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. has a .485 postseason OPS, and Matt Olsen’s is .543. On the Dodgers’ side, Ohtani, Betts and Will Smith have combined for three hits in 21 at-bats.
Those numbers don’t bode well when facing aces. The first team to two runs may win Game 3.
Milwaukee Brewers at San Diego Padres first five innings market
Why the Padres could win the first five innings
Probability: 47% at Polymarket
The Padres have been striking early throughout the postseason. They have scored first in all four games and have held 2-0 leads in each game in this series.
The Padres have been one of the most dominant teams at home this year, too. They went 51-30 at Petco Park during the regular season and had no trouble rolling the Cubs in the Wild Card round.
Plus, Dustin May is by far the Brewers’ shakiest starting pitcher. He has good career numbers against the Padres (3.14 ERA in 86 innings) but also may be nervous since this will be his first postseason appearance in six years.
Why the Brewers could win the first five innings
Probability: 37% at Kalshi
Milwaukee’s offense has been slow to get going in the series, but it can keep the momentum after its emotional win over the Padres and closer Mason Miller in Game 2.
May may not get more than three innings, but the Brewers bullpen has been awesome, especially in this series. Milwaukee has not allowed any runs in nine innings.
If May can hold down San Diego for one turn through the order, the Brewers can win the first five innings and Game 3.
How prediction markets work for MLB Playoffs trading
All prediction market trades are peer-to-peer, meaning you need a fellow user to buy and sell shares.
Users buy ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ shares on sports results. Each share costs $0.01 to $0.99. All winning shares pay out $1. Losing shares pay out nothing. Low share prices produce bigger payouts.
You can use prediction markets like a sportsbook and wait for your game to finish, or you can use them like the registered financial exchanges they are. If you choose the latter, you can day trade outcomes by buying shares at a low price and selling higher for incremental profit.
Of course, there is risk with any way you trade on sports. Luckily, you can earn valuable site credit by claiming new-user bonuses with the top prediction market promos.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Hubo una época en la que habría sido impensable que un manager rival le lanzara con cuidado a cualquier bateador para enfrentar al venezolano Ronald Acuña Jr. Pero también hubo un momento en el que habría parecido poco realista pensar que Acuña tendría las dificultades que ha experimentado en sus últimas dos postemporadas.
“Sólo necesitamos que Ronald sea Ronald”, dijo Chris Sale, as de los Bravos. “Seré sincero, el 50 por ciento de él es mejor que la mayoría. Creo que volver a casa podría aliviar un poco esa presión, estar frente a nuestros aficionados y simplemente mantenerse relajado. Creo que cuando llegas a estas situaciones, a veces intentas hacer de más”.
Acuña sentirá el cariño de la afición local en Truist Park el martes. Intentará ayudar a Atlanta a tomar ventaja de 2-1 en esta Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional, pactada al mejor de cinco juegos.
“No me preocupa, simplemente porque su talento es tan grande que en algún momento va a aparecer”, dijo Walt Weiss, manager de los Bravos.
No es que Acuña esté atravesando una mala racha prolongada. Simplemente está en una que se magnifica bajo las brillantes luces de la postemporada. Es el mismo jugador que registró un OPS de .997 en sus últimos 26 juegos de la temporada regular.
Pero en los primeros cinco juegos de esta postemporada, Acuña batea de 18-3, con tres boletos, tres ponches y ningún extrabase. También ha aportado valor con tres bases robadas.
Cabe señalar que durante ese gran cierre de temporada no estuvo enfrentándose a diario a lanzadores de la talla de Jesús Luzardo, Cristopher Sánchez, Tarik Skubal y Blake Snell. Pero la alta calidad del pitcheo no disminuye la frustración, especialmente cuando las dificultades en postemporada se remontan más allá de la campaña actual.
“Me encanta enfrentar a lanzadores que son superestrellas”, dijo Acuña. “Cada vez que voy al plato, voy a competir. Estamos tratando de ganar. Así que estoy haciendo lo mejor que puedo. Como saben, esos pitcheos son tremendos”.
Cuando Acuña bateó .337, registró un OPS de 1.017 y se convirtió en el primer jugador de la historia en sumar al menos 70 bases robadas en una temporada de 40 jonrones en el 2023, habría sido impensable que el manager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, hiciera lo que hizo en la victoria de Atlanta en el Juego 2.
Con corredores en segunda y tercera y un out en el octavo inning, Roberts ordenó a Roki Sasaki darle un boleto intencional a Drake Baldwin para preparar un enfrentamiento entre derechos contra Acuña. Tampoco es que Baldwin haya estado encendido. Su OPS de .484 en esta postemporada es, de hecho, inferior al de Acuña (.485). Pero la decisión de Roberts de lanzarle al bateador derecho dio resultado cuando Acuña bateó un rodado para una doble matanza que puso fin a la entrada.
“Creo que cada vez que ves a alguien pasar por algo así, te solidarizas con él porque casi sientes que está tratando de hacer demasiado o poniéndose demasiada presión”, dijo Sale.
Acuña tiene un OPS de .495 en las 39 apariciones al plato que ha registrado en postemporada desde el 2023. Esa cifra lo ubica en el puesto 108 entre 121 jugadores de MLB que han acumulado al menos 35 apariciones al plato en playoffs desde entonces.
Pero ciertamente no es la única superestrella que ha atravesado malas rachas prolongadas en la postemporada.
Pete Crow-Armstrong probablemente ganará el JMV de la Liga Nacional este año. Ocupa el puesto 120 en esa misma lista, con un OPS de .342 en 37 apariciones al plato. El primera base de los Bravos, Matt Olson, ha registrado un par de temporadas de 40 jonrones o más, pero aparece justo detrás de Acuña con un OPS de .490.
“Ronald es el mejor jugador del equipo y el más talentoso”, dijo Olson. “No tiene que ser Superman. Puede impactar el juego de muchísimas maneras. Todos confiamos plenamente en el jugador que es y en su talento”.

item.content:encoded:
The Athletic has live coverage of the MLB Playoffs, including the ALDS Game 2s of White Sox vs Guardians and Yankees vs Rays.
After three days of Wild Card Series action, the dust has settled and four teams (Houston Astros, Boston Red Sox, Philadelphia Phillies and Chicago Cubs) have found themselves on an early vacation. Major League Baseball’s 12-team postseason field has been whittled to eight.
Now, the race for the World Series shifts to the next round: the Division Series. Four teams (Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Dodgers, Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers) that had first-round byes will now be in action. Additionally, while the Wild Card Series featured a best-of-three format, the Division Series will be best-of-five.
Here’s how MLB’s bracket looks right now:
You can watch the MLB playoffs on Fubo (Stream Free Now).
What is Saturday’s MLB Playoff schedule and starters?
White Sox at Guardians (AL Division Series Game 1): Hagen Smith vs. Parker Messick
First pitch: 1 p.m. ET (TBS)
After the 23-year-old Smith pitched three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series against the Astros, the White Sox turn to him for an encore performance in Game 1 of the ALDS. While the club was able to pile on six runs against the Astros in a win, it won’t be as easy against the Guardians and Messick.
An All-Star this season, Messick finished his rookie campaign with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts over 32 starts. Against the White Sox, Messick carded a 2.81 ERA in four starts (25 2/3 innings).
Braves at Dodgers (NL Division Series Game 1): TBD vs. Tarik Skubal
First pitch: 4 p.m. ET (Fox)
Having burned Chris Sale to take Thursday’s winner-take-all game against the Phillies, and with Tyler Mahle also unavailable, the Braves appear to be looking at another bullpen game.
“They’ve pitched in big situations during the season, and no matter who we really see right now in that bullpen in any situation, no matter what inning it is, we’re feeling pretty confident about them,” catcher Drake Baldwin told reporters.
The Dodgers, coming off a first-round bye, will counter with Tarik Skubal, the crown jewel acquisition of this year’s trade deadline. The AL’s reigning Cy Young Award winner has a 2.61 ERA with his new team, his final starts before reaching a highly anticipated free agency.
Yankees at Rays (AL Division Series Game 1): Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen
First pitch: 6:30 p.m. ET (TBS)
Faced with an embarrassment of riches on the pitching side, the Yankees will deploy 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner Gerrit Cole against the AL East champs. After Cole in Game 1, the Yankees will have Cam Schlittler in Game 2 and some variation of Max Fried or Carlos Rodón in Games 3 and 4, the last matchup only if necessary.
On the Tampa Bay side, Drew Rasmussen, arguably one of the most underrated aces in the sport, will get the ball at Tropicana Field. For his career, Rasmussen has a 1.81 ERA in 11 games (10 starts) against the Yankees.
Padres at Brewers (NL Division Series Game 1): Robbie Ray vs. Jacob Misiorowski
First pitch: 8:30 p.m. ET (FS1)
Saturday’s final matchup will feature two pitchers at opposite ends of their careers. On the San Diego side, Robbie Ray, the 2021 AL Cy Young Award winner, has been largely unable to replicate the success he had that season. After a deadline trade from the San Francisco Giants to the Padres, Ray has carded a 5.02 ERA over nine starts.
For the Brewers, Jacob Misiorowski is just getting started. An All-Star in his rookie year, Misiorowski finished his sophomore campaign as the favorite to win the NL Cy Young Award, leading MLB with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. He’s wowed the sport with his ability to repeatedly fire fastballs in excess of 100 mph, and there’s reason to believe that, at 24 years old, his best is yet to come.
What to know about each Division Series matchup
White Sox at Guardians: The two AL Central clubs played each other 13 times during the regular season, with the White Sox winning the season series 7-6. That, however, was not enough to overcome a late surge by the Guardians and a collapse by Chicago that led to the White Sox losing control of the division and having to play their way out of the wild card.
Now, the two clubs will meet again for at least three games, a spot in the Championship Series on the line. By winning the division and finishing with a better record than the AL West winner, the Guardians were granted a first-round bye. No mind, the White Sox dispatched the Astros in two games and have been off since Thursday. That extra rest has allowed the club to realign its depleted pitching staff.
One thing to watch: How Chicago’s thin, matchup-dependent pitching staff is deployed against Cleveland’s newfound offense — the club led the AL in wRC+ (108) from Aug. 1 onward. The urgency, or lack thereof, by White Sox manager Will Venable could swing the series either direction.
Braves at Dodgers: The Braves’ pitching staff will enter Game 1 with very little margin for error, as it will likely be a group effort without a starter available. That alone could be the difference, as teams that take Game 1 in any best-of-five series have historically won the series 72 percent of the time. That said, these Dodgers have not played their best against the Braves, losing the season series 5-1, including a late-August sweep when Tyler Glasnow and Yoshinobu Yamamoto both pitched.
One thing to watch: Shohei Ohtani’s ability to contribute. The four-time MVP has spent much of the second half of the season compromised, leading to an abbreviated September, with some of it on the injured list.
“I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth, and just a little tweaks here and there, and I’ll be ready for tomorrow,” Ohtani said through interpreter Will Ireton.
Yankees at Rays: Only one team had a better record over its final 30 games than the Rays, who went 20-10 to fend off a late Yankees push to claim the AL East. That, plus a 55-26 home record that tied the Brewers for the best in MLB, has Tampa Bay inching toward its first World Series appearance since 2020. To get there, the Rays will need to beat the Yankees, who made quick work of the Red Sox in the wild-card round. That they did so without Aaron Judge on the roster or needing to call on Giancarlo Stanton in a pinch hit capacity is all the more impressive.
One thing to watch: Junior Caminero was 20 years old the last time the Rays made the postseason, going hitless in two at-bats. Since then, Caminero, now 23, has morphed into a perennial All-Star, hitting 40 home runs in consecutive seasons, the latter of which should earn him major MVP consideration. Few players love the big stage as much as Caminero. One of those players just so happens to be Cam Schlittler, the presumptive AL Cy Young Award winner, who will take the ball at least once this series. How these two match up will be one of the best subplots of this postseason.
Padres at Brewers: In a battle between arguably MLB’s hottest team (the Padres) and the league’s best team all season (the Brewers), there will be a lot of firsts. This is San Diego’s first Division Series under new owners José E. Feliciano and his wife and business partner Kwanza Jones. It will be the first extended runway for Padres rookie catcher Ethan Salas. It will be the first postseason series for Christian Yelich as the Brewers’ captain. And it will be the first time Misiorowski faces these Padres since May.
Should Milwaukee win, it will be the first time in franchise history that the club has made it to back-to-back league championship series. If San Diego upsets MLB’s No. 1 team, it will be the club’s first trip since 2022 and just its fourth overall.
One thing to watch: The bullpens. Behind multiple high-leverage arms, San Diego has made the late innings nearly impossible for opposing teams. If there’s one club that can match the Padres in that regard, it’s the Brewers. The late innings will likely be the deciding factor in who advances.

item.description: Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation Pitching wins championships. item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)
LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Andrew Painter
Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.
Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).
The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.
2. New York Yankees
11 of 12
RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP)
LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP)
RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 131 K, 127.0 IP)
LHP Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 91 K, 84.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Will Warren
With AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and three established veteran starters capable of frontline production in Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, the Yankees rotation is capable of making a major impact in October.
Schlittler logged a 1.26 ERA over 14.1 innings last October, including eight scoreless frames against the rival Red Sox in the Wild Card Round. He will now be asked to shoulder a heavier load.
It remains to be seen who the odd-man out would be in a series that calls for a three-man staff, though Rodón has made his case with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 25.1 innings in September.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
12 of 12
RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9, 2.53 ERA, 0.87 WHIP, 182 K, 185.0 IP)
LHP Tarik Skubal (4-2, 2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 60 K, 55.0 IP)
LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 52 K, 38.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Glasnow (5-2, 3.53 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 98 K, 74.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Emmet Sheehan, LHP Justin Wrobleski
The Dodgers have once again navigated much of the regular season without Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, but they are healthy rolling into October and poised to round out the playoff rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto and deadline pickup Tarik Skubal.
The starting rotation logged a 2.68 ERA over 104 innings last postseason, with Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow starting 13 of 17 games and the rest going to Shohei Ohtani, who will be limited to DH duties but has been sufficiently replaced by a two-time Cy Young winner in Skubal.
Right-hander Emmet Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA and 24 strikeouts over 17 innings in three September starts. He will serve as a multi-inning weapon out of the bullpen.

item.content:encoded:
Will we be able to see Kim Ha-seong (Atlanta Braves) and Kim Hye-seong (LA Dodgers) face off on the big league postseason stage? Kim Hye-seong looks likely to join the postseason roster for a second consecutive year.
North American sports outlet 'The Athletic' included Kim Hye-seong's name when projecting the Dodgers' division series roster on the 3rd (Korea time).
Defensive utility ability and his quick feet are the reasons Kim Hye-seong is expected to be included on the postseason roster. The outlet predicted a 26-man roster composed of 15 position players and 11 pitchers. The position player entries would be two catchers (Will Smith, Hunter Pﬂueger), four infielders (Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Max Muncy), three outfielders (Teoscar Hernández, Kyle Tucker, Andy Pages), two utilities (Tommy Edman, Kiké Hernández), and one designated hitter (Shohei Ohtani). It also projected that rookie Hosuey de Paula would take on the pinch-hitting role and Kim Hye-seong would serve as a pinch runner.
Reporter Fabian Ardaya explained, "Kim Hye-seong being on this list is not because of his hitting. He can run faster than anyone in the infield group, the oldest position group in Major League Baseball. Also, if late in the game the team inserts Hosuey de Paula and must remove one player to make two substitutions, Kim Hye-seong can cover infield defense."
Reporter KT Woo said, "Do you want an example that shows how important one stolen base can be in the postseason? Then ask manager Dave Roberts." Roberts recorded a steal that will be remembered in postseason history. The comment projected that Kim Hye-seong could be used as a late-game joker.
Kim Hye-seong finished the season in Triple-A after failing to return to the major leagues since May. His Triple-A performance was not very good either. But with everyone aware of Kim Hye-seong's speed, there is a mood that does not ignore his utility as a short-series specialist.
Manager Roberts is deliberating. At a press conference with local reporters on the 3rd he explained, "The point to consider is bench resources. We have to decide which additional players to take, whether to include a pinch runner. We're trying to coordinate that. The final bullpen pitcher spot is also under consideration."
If Kim Hye-seong is included in the division series roster, we could see a Korean derby in the postseason alongside Atlanta's Kim Ha-seong. Kim Ha-seong was already included on the Philadelphia Phillies' wild-card series roster and started in games 1 and 2.
Philadelphia started left-handed starters Jesus Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez, giving the right-handed Kim Ha-seong opportunities in a platoon role. For now, the Dodgers' Game 1 starter is also left-hander Tarik Skubal. Blake Snell is also expected to start Game 2. In that case, Kim Ha-seong could appear in both starting lineups.

Nonetheless, one potential guy could fill that need: Los Angeles Dodgers starter Tarik Skubal. While New York can spend the money under owner Steve Cohen, the question is whether he and Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns want to commit to the long-term contract and money Skubal will demand. Although the Mets need an ace, Underscore Media's Sal Licata believes that New York shoul
item.content:encoded:
The New York Mets are in offseason mode and are lacking a true ace to anchor their starting rotation. Nonetheless, one potential guy could fill that need: Los Angeles Dodgers starter Tarik Skubal.
While New York can spend the money under owner Steve Cohen, the question is whether he and Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns want to commit to the long-term contract and money Skubal will demand.
Although the Mets need an ace, Underscore Media's Sal Licata believes that New York should stay away from Skubal, given that the team will still have significant holes on the roster.
"In this particular spot, do you think Tarik Skubal alone is the difference-maker for the Mets? I don't," Licata said in an Oct. 1 Underscore Media video on X. "I think they need more than one guy atop their rotation, and if you're telling me that there are going to be at least some kind of limitations, and forget the collective bargaining agreement, all that stuff, if there is going to be some kind of limitations.
"There always are; even Steve Cohen has his limit. It's stupid to have the luxury tax threshold and not be able to go out and balance the team out if you need to. You don't want to just go all in on three freaking players. It just doesn't work."
Mets Urged to Follow Yankees Path
Moreover, Licata believes the Mets should take the approach the New York Yankees did when they didn't re-sign Juan Soto and opted to spread that money around rather than pay one guy.
"If that's going to be a thing, then why wouldn't you rather spread that out a little bit?" Licata added. "In theory, do what the Yankees did after they lost out on Soto and spread it out a little bit and allow you to add multiple pieces."
Tarik Skubal Could Pitch in Major Market Like New York
Meanwhile, SNY's Keith Raad says that if the Mets do make a serious run at Skubal in free agency, they wouldn't have to worry about the veteran ace having that shock of pitching in a big market. Skubal spent most of his career with the Detroit Tigers, but his midseason trade to the Dodgers shows he can perform for a team in a big market and with expectations.
"Skubal has been there and done that a little bit, even though he's pitched in Detroit and the fact that he's pitching well for the Dodgers as the guy in the trade shows me that he would be fine," Raad said in an Oct. 1 appearance on SNY.
"The only cautionary tale I would have is, again, Mets in-house; they brought in people, they brought in players that maybe started to go south. They have not been able to get them right. That's the part that the Mets need to figure out in player acquisition. Can we get them back to the back of the baseball card, just a simple average of who they are?"
Since the trade to the Dodgers, Skubal is 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 appearances, per StatMuse.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Mets Issued Clear Free Agency Message on Dodgers' Tarik Skubal appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] What WAR Tells Us about the Dodgers' Postseason Prospects
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers’ roster gives opposing managers plenty to worry about, and WAR helps explain why. It also gives Dodger fans a reason to appreciate players whose contributions can get overshadowed by the biggest names on the marquee. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers’ roster gives opposing managers plenty to worry about, and WAR helps explain why. It also gives Dodger fans a reason to appreciate players whose contributions can get overshadowed by the biggest names on the marquee. Put hitting, pitching, defense and baserunning on a common scale, and the picture becomes more interesting than a collection of home run totals and earned run averages.
MLB’s projected playoff rosters rank Milwaukee first (53.7 WAR), Los Angeles second (52.0); Dodgers free-agent acquisitions account for 24.5. That makes for an intriguing October argument: how much should we trust the accumulated value of a roster when the season becomes a succession of short series?
First, it helps to understand what the number actually means.
WAR stands for Wins Above Replacement. It estimates how many additional wins a player contributes compared with a readily available replacement, such as a minor league free agent. A four-WAR player has provided roughly four wins beyond that baseline over his playing time. The comparison uses a standardized replacement level, rather than whoever happens to be sitting on his team’s bench.
For position players, FanGraphs combines batting, baserunning and fielding contributions, expressed in runs. It adjusts for position, league and ballpark, incorporates the replacement-level baseline, and converts those runs into wins. Roughly speaking, about 10 additional runs are worth one win, although the conversion varies with the scoring environment. Position matters because filling a demanding defensive assignment carries value that a batting line alone cannot capture.
Pitchers require a different calculation. FanGraphs starts with Fielding Independent Pitching, emphasizing strikeouts, walks, hit batters and home runs, with an adjustment for infield flies. It accounts for ballpark, innings and the different roles of starters and relievers, then converts performance above replacement into wins. Relievers also receive a leverage adjustment reflecting the situations in which they pitch. Consequently, a pitcher’s ERA and his WAR can tell somewhat different stories.
These are FanGraphs figures, commonly called fWAR. Baseball-Reference uses a different calculation, particularly for pitchers, so its totals can differ. WAR is also an estimate: a few tenths of a win should never end an argument about which player is better.
Here are the Dodgers’ leading contributors on the FanGraphs leaderboard:
| Player | 2026 Dodgers WAR |
|---|---|
| Shohei Ohtani | 6.6 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 4.7 |
| Andy Pages | 4.5 |
| Max Muncy | 4.2 |
| Mookie Betts | 3.7 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2.7 |
| Tanner Scott | 2.4 |
| Tyler Glasnow | 2.4 |
| Tarik Skubal | 2.2 |
| Justin Wrobleski | 1.9 |
| Blake Snell | 1.9 |
FanGraphs figures through the regular season, accessed September 29. Skubal’s entry reflects his Dodgers work.
Ohtani’s total combines 3.7 WAR as a position player with 2.9 on the mound. Yamamoto supplied his value across 185 innings. Pages and Muncy both cleared four wins, an excellent reminder to give them their share of the credit. Scott’s placement alongside Glasnow is striking, too, given how much less opportunity relievers generally have to accumulate value.
For October, the workload details deserve attention: Glasnow accumulated his total in 74 innings, Snell in 42⅔ and Skubal in 62 for Los Angeles. Their season totals describe what they contributed over those opportunities; a postseason rotation presents a different distribution of innings.
That is where I find the strongest argument for the Dodgers. A playoff team can concentrate its innings among its best available pitchers. If those arms are healthy and effective, the version of a club taking the field in October can be considerably more dangerous than its season-long totals suggest. The same principle works in reverse when an important contributor is unavailable.
I would take the Dodgers’ combination of options into any series with confidence. Having several plausible game-changers gives a manager room to respond when an opponent neutralizes one part of the roster. It also gives the lineup a chance to survive a quiet series from a star.
Still, picking Los Angeles over any individual opponent is a different proposition from picking it over the entire field. Every additional round creates another opportunity for a brilliant opposing starter, a costly mistake or a badly timed slump to decide things. WAR can help establish expectations; October still gets to write the results.
For Dodger fans, these numbers support optimism and an appreciation of how many players have helped put the club in this position. The roster has enough talent to make a championship a reasonable expectation. Turning that expectation into another parade remains the most difficult part.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers postseason primer: Where do Shohei Ohtani and everyone else stand as they go for a three-peat?

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers' quest for a three-peat begins in earnest on Saturday with Game 1 of the NLDS, as they seek to become the first time since the 1998-2000 New York Yankees to complete a trilogy of titles.
Up to this point, the path for L.A. hasn't been entirely straightforward. There have been times when the Dodgers have looked a bit rickety, and that's to say nothing about everything happening off the field. They are also arguably the most talented team in the playoffs and are coming off another 100-win season.
No matter how you slice it, this is a club with more than its fair share of questions. Let's get into them, starting with the easier ones.
Who are the Dodgers playing in the NLDS?
The Dodgers will face the NL East champion Atlanta Braves, who defeated the Philadelphia Phillies in a three-game wild-card series. The Dodgers went 1-5 against Atlanta in the regular season, getting outscored 26-15.
The winner of the best-of-five series gets the victor of the other NLDS between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres.
When do the Dodgers play?
Here's the full NLDS schedule:
| Game | Date | Time (ET) | Channel | Location |
| 1 | Oct. 3 | 4 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
| 2 | Oct. 4 | 8 p.m. | FS1 | L.A. |
| 3 | Oct. 6 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 4* | Oct. 7 | 6 p.m. | FS1 | Atlanta |
| 5* | Oct. 9 | 8 p.m. | Fox | L.A. |
*if necessary
What will the Dodgers' postseason lineup be?
The Dodgers finished the season shuffling their lineup depending on the handedness of the opposing starting pitcher, and it stands to reason that they will continue doing so in the postseason.
Here's how they could line up against right-handed pitchers:
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Andy Pages, CF
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Shohei Ohtani has never hit in a batting order position other than leadoff in his MLB postseason career, but lately he has been hitting second against left-handers while Mookie Betts takes his old position atop the order.
Here's L.A.'s left-handed unit:
- Mookie Betts, SS
- Shohei Ohtani, DH
- Freddie Freeman, 1B
- Will Smith, C
- Teoscar Hernández, LF
- Kyle Tucker, RF
- Andy Pages, CF
- Max Muncy, 3B
- Tommy Edman, 2B
Both of those orders alternate left-right all the way down to Edman, a switch-hitter at the bottom. It's entirely possible the Dodgers go a different route, too.
What will the Dodgers' postseason rotation be?
That's fairly settled. The Dodgers will trot out the quartet of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. The order in which those arms are utilized remains to be seen, though the Dodgers have every reason to maximize innings for Yamamoto after what he did last year.
How has this season gone for the Dodgers?
It has gone well, by the standards of any other team.
By the standards of the Dodgers, well, there are a few dynamics at play. This is a good baseball team. They probably should've been better this season, and not just because they have the largest payroll in history, at a projected $410 million, per Roster Resource.
A two-time World Series champion filled its two biggest roster holes by giving two players, Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz, the highest salaries in the history of their positions. Entering the season, the Dodgers were estimated by the usually conservative PECOTA projections from Baseball Prospectus to win 104 games, and that didn't take into account acquiring a two-time reigning Cy Young Award winner in Skubal and more at the MLB trade deadline.
So in that sense, 100 wins is a disappointment. One of the most talented teams in MLB history (on paper at least) had more than its fair share of injuries, underperformances and mistakes. There was a point when the club seemed on the verge of letting the NL West become a race, as the Arizona Diamondbacks halved a division lead from 14 games to seven in the span of about a month between July and August, but then the D-backs got mired in their own slump and the Dodgers got hot again.
Overall, the Dodgers' issues boiled down to an offense that slumped hard in July and August, rough days for starting pitchers who will not be starting games in the playoffs and an epically bad bullpen night here and there. The first of those got better in September, though, which you can read more about here.
There is also the Dodgers' 38-37 record against teams with winning records this season, as their worst stretches of the year coincided with some of their toughest road trips and homestands, and that can leave an impression. Of course, it's a bit silly to worry about a team handling its business against good teams when it's going for a three-peat.
How does this team compare to last year's?
It's easy to remember the 2024 and 2025 Dodgers as juggernauts, but both of those teams had flaws that easily could've been fatal.
The 2024 Dodgers entered the postseason with a three-man rotation of Yamamoto, Walker Buehler and Jack Flaherty, with Clayton Kershaw, Glasnow, Dustin May, Gavin Stone, River Ryan and Emmet Sheehan among the starting pitchers on the injured list.
That team was so desperate for starting pitching help that it went full bullpen game while facing elimination at the hands of the Padres in the NLDS. It was only through the grace of a deep and competent bullpen that L.A. triumphed.
The 2025 team had the opposite problem. No one was doubting a rotation of Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow and Ohtani, but there were most certainly concerns about a bullpen whose late-inning arms consistently blew games well into September.
Once again, the Dodgers adjusted. With their rotation overflowing, they turned to a number of starting pitchers to fill the gaps. Every single pitcher who appeared in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series started at least nine games for this year's team.
With that in mind, the 2026 Dodgers might be the franchise's most balanced roster to enter the postseason in years, but there is once again a major question.
It's Ohtani. Let's get into that.
How's Shohei Ohtani doing?
Ohtani was the overwhelming NL MVP front-runner for the first half of this season, having begun the year as both a hitter and a pitcher for the first time in his Dodgers career.
Then Ohtani's knee started barking in July, resulting in the team taking him off the mound and giving him a lubricant injection during the All-Star break. He also developed a biceps issue at some point.
Those injuries didn't immediately stop Ohtani from playing. Much like he did in his recovery from internal brace surgery in 2024 and 2025, Ohtani played as the Dodgers' every-day designated hitter while rehabbing. However, the injuries clearly started to affect him in September, and the Dodgers opted to put him on the injured list for the first time in his tenure with the team.
Ohtani returned with five games left in the regular season and went 5-for-21 with 1 walk, 8 strikeouts and one extra-base hit, a double. Those numbers clearly aren't up to his standards, but if there's a reason for optimism, it's that he hit batted balls with exit velocities of 106.8, 106, 103.9 and 103.4 mph. He hadn't hit a ball that hard since August. Of course, the flip side of that optimism is maybe a 100% version of him would've hit them even harder.
Since his return, the Dodgers have insisted that Ohtani is feeling better, with hitting coach Aaron Bates saying Thursday that they had absolutely no concerns. The ship has sailed on Ohtani pitching again this season, though.
It still feels like Ohtani is the single biggest question for the Dodgers entering this postseason, given how long-term his knee issue has been. He at least got plenty of rest between his 15-day IL stint and the five days off between the end of the regular season and the start of the NLDS.
Do the Dodgers have a young, dynamic replacement at DH if Ohtani isn't healthy?
What an oddly specific question. The answer is yes, potentially.
It's not a stretch to say that Josue De Paula was the best hitting prospect in baseball at the time of his promotion to fill Ohtani's roster spot in September. At the time, every other position player in the MLB Pipeline top 10 was a shortstop who could offer significant two-way value, while De Paula will eventually be a bat-first corner outfielder at best and a bat-only first baseman at worst.
The good news is De Paula definitely looked like he belonged in his 11 games with the Dodgers while Ohtani was on the IL, slashing .323/.500/.581 and helping inject life into a previously struggling lineup. He was optioned when Ohtani came back, the timing of which made him available for the start of the NLDS.
In the playoffs, De Paula is likely to be the Dodgers' top left-handed bat off the bench, and he could fit in at designated hitter or corner outfield if someone gets hurt. It seems highly unlikely, however, that the Dodgers will take any plate appearances from Ohtani, barring a significant aggravation of that knee issue.
Are Kyle Tucker and Edwin Díaz still having horrifically bad debut seasons for the Dodgers?
Those two players were the butt of jokes all season after they signed record contracts to join the defending champions, then posted the worst seasons of their careers. However, both offered reason for optimism in September.
Tucker entered the month slashing .228/.326/.357 but finished the season at .262/.354/.536, numbers more in line with what the Dodgers were expecting when they signed him to a four-year, $240 million contract. His six homers in September were double what he had in any other month of the season.
In 2026, Díaz made seven appearances with a 10.50 ERA, spent three months on the injured list due to loose bodies in his elbow, came back for nine more appearances, posted a 12.91 ERA in those, then hit the IL one more time in August due to what was described as neck inflammation.
Then he came back in September and, like Tucker, performed like the player the Dodgers were initially expecting, with nine strikeouts and one hit allowed across five scoreless innings. Díaz no longer has the closer role, but he made as good a case as he could for late-inning work in October.
Tucker and Díaz still finished the year with horrendous numbers, and barring some postseason heroics, that's what most fans will remember. Still, it's important to know that the Dodgers might not treat them in October like their overall numbers would suggest.
How's the rest of the Dodgers' bullpen shaping up?
It's a diverse group. We've already talked about Díaz, who could be anything from middle reliever to closer by the end of the postseason. However, the current closer is Tanner Scott, who played the Díaz role last year as the high-priced reliever who struggled in his first year with the Dodgers.
Scott's second season in L.A. has gone far better. He converted 25 of 29 save attempts with a 2.69 ERA.
As for the other six spots in the bullpen, the contenders are Edgardo Henriquez, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Kris Bubic and Brock Stewart from the normal pot of relievers and Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Sheehan as overflow from the rotation.
Henriquez might be the most intriguing name from that group, as the flame-throwing right-hander was great during the regular season, only to hit the IL due to lower back discomfort in September. The Dodgers think he's trending toward playing in the NLDS.
Does a Dodgers World Series guarantee a salary cap?
You'd think. Some certainly seem to think. However, let's take a view rooted not in optimism but in realism.
The owners want a salary cap. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani signed on the dotted line of a $700 million contract. They wanted one before Shohei Ohtani was born (what else happened in 1994?). They want a salary cap for the same reason every owner in sports has wanted a salary cap — not for competitive balance but to remove pressure on them to spend like they want to compete.
The Dodgers have made for a convenient boogeyman by being baseball's biggest spender and baseball's best team over the past several years. They must be stopped to save baseball, or so the argument goes, as no team is supposed to have L.A.'s combination of resources, competence and aggression. It's just not fair. It almost goes without saying in many discussions that the point of a salary cap is to end the Dodgers' unfair dynasty.
And yet, it really needs to be noted: Commissioner Rob Manfred does not fantasize about the Dodgers being forced to dismantle their tremendous machine — of Andrew Friedman, on his knees, begging a small-market team to take Glasnow's contract off his books — like some salary-cap proponents seem to do. Ohtani winning rings on the Dodgers has worked out quite nicely for baseball. A salary cap can be introduced for cost control and the veneer of parity, but MLB ultimately benefits from the large-market teams being contenders with the biggest stars. As such, it's hard to imagine a salary cap being introduced in such a way that the Dodgers, Yankees, Mets and other top spenders are forced to take immediate action to get below a line. A slow introduction of a cap or some sort of contract grandfathering seems far more likely, giving the Dodgers and others time to adjust.
The Dodgers' recent success isn't so much fuel for a salary cap as it is fuel for salary-cap opinions. It has certainly convinced many fans of a salary cap's necessity, but the MLBPA is playing cards at a different table. They don't want a salary cap, no matter what the Dodgers do, and they and the MLB owners are ultimately the people whose opinions matter here.
Limitations on the Dodgers would merely be a byproduct of MLB getting what it wants, and that would be completely antithetical to the history of the union. It's difficult to imagine the next month impacting salary-cap discussions to any significant degree.
What about the money problems with Dodgers ownership?
That's still in progress, and it remains unclear how much it will affect the Dodgers.
The short version of a very complicated story is that the companies operated by Dodgers majority owner Mark Walter were found to be doing business with one another at a rate much greater than what they were telling customers, investors and regulators. Walter is now facing considerable legal scrutiny and has reacted by selling whatever he can to pay off some of the loans that turned out to be less than kosher.
His biggest move was to sell his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers at a franchise valuation of $12.5 billion, one year after buying the team at a $10 billion valuation. He has also offloaded his stake in the Premier League club Chelsea and the Ligue 1 club Strasbourg.
Those were big parts of Walter's sports portfolio, which also includes the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks, the Cadillac Formula 1 team, the entire Professional Women's Hockey League and, of course, the Dodgers.
Dodgers leadership has repeatedly said the team isn't for sale. Of course, any sale would probably come out of nowhere — the Lakers' move was dropped on an otherwise uneventful Wednesday morning — but for now, that's mere speculation with the Dodgers.
One notable sign of trouble in Chavez Ravine, though, was a report that Walter recently approached Charter Communications about letting them out of their famously expensive Dodgers (and Lakers) contracts in exchange for a lump sum payout. It appears nothing has come out of that, but those are not stories you hear when everything is going well.
All of that's to say that Walter would likely welcome the immediate financial benefit of winning a third straight World Series even more than your typical billionaire. Of course, that outcome isn't up to him.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] Phillies Could Trade Kyle Schwarber This Winter? 5 Potential Destinations After New Speculation, Including the NY Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jasonburgosmma; Jason Burgos
item.description: After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a notable MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading star slugger Kyle Schwarber this winter. The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations.
