item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a notable MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading star slugger Kyle Schwarber this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star DH. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract with four years and $120 million left on the deal.
While it is likely Schwarber is playing for the Phillies in 2027 and beyond, especially since he has a full no-trade clause, if the team did look to trade him this winter, here are five teams he could end up going to in the offseason.
Detroit Tigers
After trading top star Tarik Skubal before this season’s trade deadline, the Detroit Tigers will probably be open to diverting the money they were willing to give the reigning American League Cy Young to a different star.
While the Tigers are in greater need of elite pitching, adding one of the best sluggers in the game would be a massive addition for their lineup in 2027. Furthermore, after trading the two-time All-Star ace in the summer, they certainly now have the prospect assets that would interest the Phillies.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Schwarber available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. The idea of Schwarber and Guerrero Jr. in the same batting order will give other AL East pitching staffs a cold sweat.
New York Yankees
The New York Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, Aaron Judge and Schwarber in the same lineup would be the most terrifying back-to-back in baseball.
Cincinnati Reds
To the surprise of many, the Cincinnati Reds were serious about bringing Schwarber back to his native Ohio this past offseason. And the 33-year-old was allegedly open to the idea as well. However, the draw of playing for a title contender he was familiar with and a huge contract brought him back to Philadelphia. The Reds would have some solid youngsters to offer in a trade, including top prospects that got the call to the big leagues this year.
Boston Red Sox
After a disappointing performance in the playoffs, it would not be a surprise if the Boston Red Sox looked to make a major move or two this winter. They don’t have an obvious DH for next season, so Schwarber would fill a clear need. Furthermore, slotting him into the middle of their batting order would make life far easier and offer more opportunities for Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, and Adley Rutschman to drive in runs.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers set their trade deadline sights on one big target and landed him in Tarik Skubal. The two-time Cy Young Award winner will get the call to start Game 1 of the National League Division Series on Saturday at Dodger Stadium against the Atlanta Braves.
Fabian Ardaya at The Athletic was first to report Skubal getting the call in Game 1.
Skubal started two Games 1 with the Detroit Tigers, and in six postseason starts over 2024-25 has a 2.04 ERA with 56 strikeouts against five unintentional walks in 39 2/3 innings, and has lasted at least six innings in all six starts.
When the Dodgers acquired Skubal from the Tigers on August 2, president of baseball operations noted the team's singular focus at this year's trade deadline.
"We were of the mind to be aggressive for one player, and fortunately we were able to line up," Friedman said at the time. "As we've talked about a lot, whenever there's a star-level player available who can really shift championship odds, those are the moments we'll be more aggressive."
Yoshinobu Yamamoto started Game 1 of the 2024 NLDS, and is coming off one of the best postseasons in MLB history, 5-1 with a 1.45 ERA in 37 1/3 innings. That included consecutive complete games in the NLCS and World Series, and he won all three of his appearances in the Fall Classic, including getting the final eight outs of Game 7 one day after starting and pitching six innings to win Game 6.
Blake Snell has five career starts in Game 1, including twice for the Dodgers last year in the wild card round and NLCS. Tyler Glasnow, with four career Game 1 starts, rounds out the rotation.
"To be honest, we can kind of really put all four guys in a hat, and run them out there," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday.
"Our pitching staff is pretty special, in my opinion," first baseman Freddie Freeman said. "We got four number ones rolling out there, with Yama, Snell, Skubs, and Glasnow."
Skubal has been just about everything the Dodgers could have wanted when they traded for the two-time Cy Young Award winner on August 2. In 10 starts with Los Angeles, the left-hander had a 2.61 ERA and 2.84 xERA with 70 strikeouts and 13 walks in 62 innings.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers rotation is their greatest strength this October
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers won a championship in 2024 with a decimated starting rotation and dominant bullpen, then flipped the script with a stellar rotation buoying a shaky bullpen to win another title in 2025. This year the Dodgers might have melded the two heading into October.
"We have a lot of really talented arms," general manager Brandon Gomes said Tuesday. "I think this is about as deep of a pitching staff as we've ever had. There's a lot of really good options to work through as a group."
For now, we'll focus on the rotation, which looks just as strong this year as it did last October, even though Shohei Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3 and will not pitch this postseason. The Dodgers filled that slot with a two-time Cy Young Award winner, trading for Tarik Skubal on August 2.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto was again the rock of the starting rotation, making every start for the second year in a row. Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow each missed multiple months with a long injured-list stint in season, then returned with enough of a runway to get ready for October. All four put up solid numbers this season.
| Pitcher | Starts | IP | ERA | xERA | BB rate | K rate |
| Skubal | 26 | 158.7 | 2.72 | 2.94 | 4.4% | 30.0% |
| Yamamoto | 28 | 185 | 2.53 | 2.94 | 5.9% | 25.7% |
| Snell | 9 | 62 | 1.90 | 2.17 | 9.2% | 31.8% |
| Glasnow | 13 | 74 | 3.53 | 2.86 | 8.7% | 34.0% |
*Skubal's numbers include Tigers & Dodgers
"To be honest, we can kind of really put all four guys in a hat, and run them out there," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday.
Last year, Yamamoto, Snell, Ohtani, and Glasnow combined to start all 17 postseason games, and put up a collective 2.55 ERA in 113 innings, with 127 strikeouts and a 28.5-percent strikeout rate. All four of them pitched in Game 7 of the World Series, including Yamamoto getting the final eight outs one day after winning Game 6 as the starter. Yamamoto last October pitched the Dodgers' first two postseason compete games since 1988, and Blake Snell had starts of eight and seven innings as well.
Quality starts are a bit crude, but criticism tends to focus on the minimum requirements — at least six innings, with no more than three earned runs allowed. But across MLB this regular season, teams went 1,094-484 (.693) in games when they got a quality start, with a collective 1.74 ERA from the starters in those games.
This season, the Dodgers led the majors with 83 quality starts, eight more than the next-best team, the Philadelphia Phillies. Those 83 quality starts by the Dodgers this year were their most since 2015, when they got 95 quality starts from a rotation that included the second- and third-place finishers in National League Cy Young Award voting (Zack Greinke, Clayton Kershaw). They were 60-23 (.723) when getting a quality start in 2026.
Dodgers starters last postseason had 10 quality starts, more than any pitching staff since the 2013 Detroit Tigers. Those 10 quality starts in 17 games were one more than the Dodgers had in their previous five postseasons combined, totaling 53 games.
Last postseason, the Dodgers won all 10 of the games in which they received a quality start, with zero or one run allowed by the starter in seven of those games. Two of those quality starts were by Ohtani, but he's replaced in the rotation by Skubal, who last postseason posted three quality starts in his three tries, totaling 36 strikeouts and four runs allowed in his 20 2/3 innings for the Detroit Tigers.
"Watching Tarik Skubal pitch in the playoffs last year was must-see TV. I was in awe, watching the energy, the dominance he exhibited there," Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said in August after trading for Skubal. "I can't wait to see it on our club."

The New York Yankees were cited as being "just behin
item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal's New Landing Spots Predicted by Insiders Ahead of MLB Free Agency
As Tarik Skubal prepares for his first postseason with the Los Angeles Dodgers, people within MLB are also looking ahead to his free agency and which team he might end up signing with.
In a survey of MLB insiders conducted by ESPN's Kiley McDaniel, the Dodgers, New York Mets and Detroit Tigers were cited as the "true contenders" for the two-time AL Cy Young winner.
The New York Yankees were cited as being "just behind" the lead group in how often they were mentioned.
In the group of sleepers, McDaniel listed the Chicago White Sox, San Diego Padres and Los Angeles Angels as teams that frequently came up.
The Tigers, who traded Skubal to Los Angeles on Aug. 2, are the most interesting of the top group because they don't usually play in the deep end of the free-agent pool.
If they were going to sign Skubal, the Tigers could have just done it last offseason to avoid reaching the point where they had to trade him. He told USA Today's Bob Nightengale during spring training there was "no offer" that came from Detroit.
The Dodgers aren't a surprise given Skubal is already there and they have a habit of signing the best free agent every year, but McDaniel did note the respondents had "some hesitation" about including them given the uncertainty around their ownership situation with Mark Walter at the moment.
Even though Walter sold his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers earlier this year just 10 months after his purchase was finalized, Dodgers officials have strongly maintained the MLB club is not being sold.
It will be interesting to see how aggressive the Mets want to be this offseason after a 74-88 record in 2026. They spent almost $240 million in free agency last winter, but fans were unhappy about the ways they invested their money.
Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns could also be feeling a lot of pressure given that he was at the center of a lot of vitriol from fans in Queens for things like not even attempting to bring back Pete Alonso before he signed with the Baltimore Orioles.
Among the three sleeper teams listed by McDaniel, the White Sox stand out as a team that could make a huge leap to being a top-tier AL team if they upgrade their rotation. The offense ranked fifth in runs scored and sixth in homers this season.
The Angels are in a fascinating position because Stan Kroenke is set to take over as owner after agreeing to buy the club from Arte Moreno for $3.9 billion.
Kroenke's purchase still has to be approved and the timing of that could impact how aggressive they are in free agency, but it's not uncommon for a new ownership team to want to make an aggressive splash right out of the gate.
The downside, though, is the Angels are so far away from being a contender after losing a franchise-record 100 games with a middling farm system, albeit one that is improving, that giving a huge sum of money to Skubal right now may not be the best team-building strategy even if it would make them more interesting in the short-term.
Skubal finished the 2026 regular season with a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts in 158.2 innings over 26 starts between the Tigers and Dodgers. This was his fourth consecutive season with a sub-3.00 ERA and at least 10.0 strikeouts per nine innings.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers to tab new ace in surprise Game 1 playoff rotation decision
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris
item.description: To begin their quest for a third-straight World Series this postseason, the Dodgers will turn to the one pitcher in their rotation yet to win a championship ring. Tarik Skubal is expected to be named the team’s starter for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, a source with knowledge of the situation told the California Post, giving the reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner and marquee trade deadline acquisition an immediate opportunity to jump-s
item.content:encoded:
To begin their quest for a third-straight World Series this postseason, the Dodgers will turn to the one pitcher in their rotation yet to win a championship ring.
Tarik Skubal is expected to be named the team’s starter for Game 1 of the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves on Saturday, a source with knowledge of the situation told the California Post, giving the reigning two-time Cy Young Award winner and marquee trade deadline acquisition an immediate opportunity to jump-start the club’s three-peat bid.
The Dodgers, of course, had no bad options for their playoff opener.
Their rotation includes four pitchers who would be No. 1 options on most other clubs, with Skubal being joined by Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow for this year’s October push.
However, Skubal is set to get the nod, as The Athletic first reported, after increasingly impressive late-season performances with the Dodgers following his blockbuster arrival from the Detroit Tigers in August.
The 29-year-old left-hander posted a 5-2 record and 2.61 ERA in 10 post-deadline starts with the club, improving upon the 7-5 mark and 2.79 ERA he had with the Tigers during a first half that was sidetracked by an elbow procedure that sidelined him for all of May.
Skubal’s best outings came in the final weeks of the regular season, when he spun a pair of scoreless seven-inning starts in two of his final three appearances of the campaign.
Prior to Friday’s news, there was a thought that Yamamoto would be the Dodgers’ Game 1 starter, given his World Series MVP heroics last fall.
But Yamamoto threw extensively in a simulated game on Wednesday, during the club’s bye week workouts. That kept him on his customary once-per-week pitching schedule (his regular-season finale came on the Wednesday before that) and might line him up to pitch in Game 3 in Atlanta next Tuesday instead. Of note: Yamamoto has notably better splits on the road (1.77 ERA) than at home (3.13 ERA) this year.
Snell, who has followed Skubal in the Dodgers’ rotation lately, seems like the logical candidate to start Game 2 on Sunday. Glasnow, who pitched in another simulated game Thursday, figures to go in Game 4, and could be an option out of the bullpen this weekend.
While Skubal –– who will be the sport’s top free agent this winter –– has yet to win a World Series, he does have a sterling postseason track record.
In six playoff outings over the last two years with the Tigers, he pitched to a 2.04 ERA while striking out 56 batters in 39 ⅔ innings. Those numbers would be even better if not for his one October clunker, when he gave up five runs in a winner-take-all loss in Game 5 of the 2024 American League Division Series.
That failure has become a motivator for Skubal in the two years since. It has left him with a feeling of unfinished business as he begins another playoff campaign amid new surroundings now.
“Once the months change and the playoffs start, nothing matters,” he said last week. “It’s just about winning that game, and that’s how I treat every single start. Because I’m just trying to put our team in a position to win a baseball game. That won’t change from today, and whenever my next start is.”

item.title: [Diario AS] Dodgers NLDS roster: Who will make the 26-man playoff roster against the Braves?
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Serrano; Jennifer Bubel
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles. Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeat
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have won the National League West for the fifth consecutive season and for the 13th time in the last 14 years. The only team to interrupt their run was the San Francisco Giants in 2021. Since then, no one has been able to take the division away from Los Angeles.
Now the defending back-to-back World Series champions are preparing for the National League Division Series, where they will face the Atlanta Braves beginning Saturday at Dodger Stadium. Atlanta advanced by defeating the Philadelphia Phillies in the Wild Card Series, setting up the Dodgers’ first postseason matchup with the Braves since the 2021 NL Championship Series.
Your 2026 Los Angeles Dodgers. pic.twitter.com/XYs9LzjRIb
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers’ five-day bye gave Dave Roberts and his staff time to prepare their roster, and while most of the pieces are already in place, there are still some important decisions to make before the 26-man NLDS roster is finalized. MLB reports that the final bench spot remains particularly unsettled, while the bullpen could also have an opening depending on the health of Edgardo Henriquez.
Who will make the Dodgers’ pitching staff?
The Dodgers’ biggest strength heading into October is their starting rotation. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, and Tyler Glasnow form a formidable group, although Roberts had not formally announced the order entering Friday.
Yamamoto is the leading candidate to start Game 1 against Atlanta. His normal rest schedule is one of the reasons the Japanese right-hander makes the most sense for the opener, as starting Saturday would also give him the chance to be available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
#ITFDB presented by Toyo Tires. pic.twitter.com/TcKpliJrnR
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 24, 2026
The Dodgers also have several pitchers who could be used in relief despite spending much of the regular season as starters. Roki Sasaki, Justin Wrobleski and Emmet Sheehan are among the options who could give Roberts additional flexibility out of the bullpen.
Edgardo Henriquez is another name to watch. The right-hander emerged as an important leverage option during the regular season before lower back discomfort ended his year prematurely. The Dodgers planned to have him face hitters during the bye, with an activation for the NLDS possible if he comes through the workout without any problems.
What will the Dodgers’ offense look like?
Shohei Ohtani will once again be the centerpiece of the Dodgers’ offense, but the situation is different from what it appeared to be when the original story was written.
Ohtani returned from the injured list in late September and played in each of the Dodgers’ final five regular-season games. He went 5-for-21 with eight strikeouts and one walk during that stretch, but Roberts said the team had no health concerns with its superstar heading into the postseason.
It’s Shotime! On this day in 2024, Shohei Ohtani started the 50/50 club.
This MomenTito’s in Dodger history presented by Tito's Handmade Vodka. pic.twitter.com/cxOEcJyPNK
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 19, 2026
Ohtani is expected to remain the designated hitter, with Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freddie Freeman at first base and Max Muncy at third. The Dodgers’ outfield is also largely established, with Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages expected to occupy the three spots.
The lineup could continue to feature some adjustments depending on the opposing starter. Against right-handed pitching, Ohtani has been used at the top of the order, while Betts has taken the leadoff spot against left-handers. That platoon is expected to continue into October.
Who's your Player of the Game? Comment your answer below! pic.twitter.com/tt6sVtGvWT
— Los Angeles Dodgers (@Dodgers) September 26, 2026
Who gets the final roster spot?
The Dodgers have several candidates competing for what could be their final bench spot: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, and Hyeseong Kim. MLB’s postseason preview identified the decision as one of the biggest remaining questions for the club.
De Paula is intriguing after his impressive first taste of the Majors. The Dodgers’ top prospect hit .323 with seven RBIs and seven runs scored in 11 games before being optioned to Triple-A when Ohtani returned from the injured list. His performance was strong enough to keep him in the postseason conversation.
But Kim offers something different. His defensive versatility, speed, and ability to contribute off the bench could make him valuable in a playoff series, particularly if Roberts wants another defensive option late in games.
MLB.com Dodgers beat reporter Sonja Chen noted that both De Paula and Kim could have a chance to make the NLDS roster if Los Angeles carries 14 position players and 12 pitchers. The final decision could ultimately come down to whether the Dodgers prefer another impact bat or additional speed and defense.
Rushing and Call remain possibilities as well, meaning the Dodgers have not simply decided between De Paula and Kim.
The other variable is the pitching staff. If Los Angeles carries only 12 pitchers rather than the maximum 13, it would open another position-player spot and potentially allow Roberts to keep more of those candidates.
Dodgers are chasing history
There is plenty more than a division title at stake for Los Angeles. The Dodgers are attempting to become the first team since the New York Yankees from 1998-2000 to win three consecutive World Series titles. They have already won three of the past six championships and enter October as the defending champions for the second straight year.
Their first obstacle is now set: the Atlanta Braves. The two teams will meet Saturday in Game 1 of the NLDS at Dodger Stadium, with Yamamoto the likely starter for Los Angeles. Before the first pitch, however, Roberts and the Dodgers still have a handful of decisions to make about exactly which players will be part of their attempt at a historic three-peat.

item.title: [FanSided] MLB Power Rankings: Every remaining playoff team after Wild Card Round
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts. The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. item.content:encoded:
With the exception of Braves-Phillies (of course), this year's Wild Card round was pretty lopsided. The competition should heat up in the Divisional Series, however. Not only are the best teams in each league being reintroduced, but we have division rivals and compelling stylistic contrasts.
The Brewers and Padres could not be more different in how their teams were built. The Rays and Yankees don't like each other. The Guardians and White Sox also don't like each other. As for Braves-Dodgers? Well, there's plenty of recent history there. But which teams have the look of title contenders as we move deeper into October? Let's rank all eight remaining teams in terms of championship equity.
8. Chicago White Sox
The White Sox made it hard on themselves down the stretch, but Chicago is riding high after a first-round sweep of the Astros, with blessings from the Pope. Coming into the postseason, the White Sox were broadly dinged for their youth and inexperience. As fate would have it, though, the South Siders were significantly more poised than a seasoned Astros team.
Chicago's lineup performed top to bottom. They worked deep into counts and made smart, situational swings. The rotation is still a mess, and the bullpen is not much better, but there's a lovable underdog quality to this White Sox team that is hard to ignore. By default, the White Sox rank last here, but an ALDS matchup with the Guardians is perfectly winnable. Do not discount the possibility of a South Siders pennant run.
7. Cleveland Guardians
Cleveland has been there and done that. This team is always the AL Central champ, it feels like, even when the odds are stacked against them. The Guardians hit much better down the stretch after a brutal start to the campaign, while their pitching is a potential superpower. Parker Messick and Gavin Williams can match just about any aces blow-for-blow, and this bullpen always tends to perform.
The question now becomes: Can Stephen Vogt's squad translate their signature Guards Ball style to October? The answer for years now has been "no." Cleveland lacks thump in the heart of the order, but tends to execute the small things — bunts, base-running, two-strike hitting — better than anyone. Chicago's pitching staff is vulnerable and the Guardians have the edge in experience, but so did Houston. And the Astros' bats were much better. The outcome of this series will not shock me in either direction, to be frank.
6. Atlanta Braves
The Braves lineup struggled down the stretch but appeared to wake up against the Phillies, especially in the clincher. Atlanta has no shortage of offensive talent and a deep bullpen, with plenty of postseason experience to draw on. So why ranked so low?
Well, the rotation is a mess. Chris Sale is an elite 1A, but Tyler Mahle is questionable against better offensive teams (see: Dodgers) and their third starter is Grant Holmes behind an opener. Atlanta has seven starters on the IL and could struggle to build a bridge to the stellar back end of their bullpen in non-Sale starts. That said, if the Braves' bats heat up, perhaps it does not matter. There is a clear break in quality between Cleveland at No. 7 and the rest of the field. The Braves are very, very capable of mounting a deep run. Atlanta notably went 5-1 against the Dodgers this season.
5. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays just kept winning all season long. There was no more consistent force in the American League. We can quibble with the back half of their lineup and question the depth of their rotation, but the Rays are an extremely disciplined club with star power (Junior Caminero) and fundamental skills (Chandler Simpson, Jonny DeLuca) in equal measure.
Tampa is going to defend at a high level and run the bases with intent. Their pitching staff does not look so fearsome on paper, but Drew Rasmussen is a bonafide ace and Freddy Peralta looked more like himself in September. Whether this team can match the raw explosiveness of the Yankees' lineup is the swing factor. On the flip side, New York has a propensity for unforced errors that Tampa can ruthlessly capitalize on.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees are still waiting on Aaron Judge. New York stuffed its Wild Card roster with platoon bats and situational hitters, but Aaron Boone probably needs more pitchers for a five-game Divisional Series. The lineup exploded against the Red Sox, but Tampa will almost certainly manage its pitching staff better than Chad Tracy and Boston did.
New York is the best team in the American League on paper, even with all their injuries, but the bullpen is perilously thin and it's hard to trust this lineup completely. Ben Rice has caught fire at an optimal moment, so there's that. And the Yankees boast, by far, the most star power of any team west of Los Angeles. Whether it can all come together against a healthy, well-rested Rays team remains to be seen.
3. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers, almost without fail, dominate the regular season despite ownership's pervasive cheapness. This team knows how to develop talent in-house and locate value on the margins. There is no better-run small-market clubhouse in MLB. And yet, Milwaukee has consistently fallen flat in the playoffs. Whether or not this year is any different comes down to a couple factors.
First, Jacob Misiorowski helps. Milwaukee has the best pitcher in baseball and he may damn near guarantee a Game 1 win in the NLDS. The Brewers' bullpen is rock solid, too, while the depth of their rotation is respectable. Milwaukee's pitching can win ballgames. More importantly, there's less elite competition than usual; even the Dodgers are scuttling at the plate, while the entire American League is poked full of holes. The path has never been clearer for the Brewers, who compensate for limited slug with impressive plate discipline and savvy situational hitting. If Milwaukee can maintain its extraordinarily high baseline, there's reason to believe this could be the year it all clicks.
2. San Diego Padres
There are few stars I trust more in a high-leverage spot than Fernando Tatis Jr. The man just makes good things happen, whether he's using his power or his speed. San Diego's entire lineup, really, has come on strong in the final month. After sputtering for much of the regular season, the likes of Jackson Merrill and Manny Machado have apparently remembered how talented they are. Gavin Sheets and Ty France are improbably major contributors. On the pitching front, Michael King and Nick Pivetta tore through a loaded Cubs lineup. The Padres' bullpen is the best in baseball, so no team can more easily build a bridge between their frontline starters and the ninth inning.
San Diego's rotation depth is suspect; once Walker Buehler and Robbie Ray are asked to carry several innings, it could get dicey. But in terms of momentum and top shelf star power, the Padres clear the majority of the competition around them. It can't hurt that San Diego plays the Dodgers as well as any team, either. That matchup could ultimately define the 2026 season, assuming the Padres can out-slug the No. 1 seed Brewers.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
This shouldn't come as a shock. The Dodgers aren't as untouchable as their reputation suggests, but there's still only one team with Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow lined up on the mound. Meanwhile, Shohei Ohtani has proven his capacity for clutch swings time after time since arriving in Hollywood two years ago. Los Angeles has the best pitchers and the best player in MLB, with a star-studded lineup to boot. Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Freddie Freeman weren't at the peak of their powers this season, but that's still a group worth trusting when every at-bat is magnified.
Los Angeles has depth, too. Josue De Paula is one of the most exciting young bats in baseball and the Dodgers barely have room for him on the roster. Alex Call and Dalton Rushing are useful as situational hitters. The primary concern is L.A.'s bullpen, but Rōki Sasaki, Kris Bubic and Justin Wrobleski — their excess rotation arms — should help the Dodgers cover innings when needed. The Dodgers are banged-up and very much vulnerable, but this is still the team to beat, full stop.

item.dc:creator: Michael Whitaker
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers, who have their eyes set on a third consecutive World Series title, acquired ace pitcher Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster trade in early August. In return for Skubal, the Dodgers sent outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith to Detroit. item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, who have their eyes set on a third consecutive World Series title, acquired ace pitcher Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers in a blockbuster trade in early August.
In return for Skubal, the Dodgers sent outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith to Detroit.
Right now, it remains to be seen whether or not the Dodgers will be able to re-sign Skubal, who can become an unrestricted free agent following the season, and is expected to potentially command upwards of $400 million on his next contract.
Los Angeles Dodgers Pitcher Tarik Skubal Makes Feelings On Expectations Clear
In an interview with Bill Shaikin of the Los Angeles Times, Skubal said he’s come to embrace the heightened expectations that come with being the reigning American League Cy Young Award winner, and having joined a club with legitimate title aspirations.
“I’ve grown to appreciate expectations from teammates, from fans, from organizations,” he said. “I’ve come to appreciate pressure. Early on in my career, there wasn’t much of that. It was more just kind of finding my footing, which I’m grateful for. It helped me learn a lot about myself.
“Having the expectation of being a team that is going to win the World Series, and me being a part of that, is something that I’ve come to really appreciate,” he continued. “I’ve come to appreciate all that stuff. As much as they can be looked at as negative things, or stress-inducing things, I’ve come to really appreciate those things, because I haven’t had that for my entire career.”
Meanwhile, he discussed his admiration for Clayton Kershaw, who played his entire 18-year MLB career with the Dodgers, winning three World Series rings.
“It takes a superhuman to be held to the standard he was being held to, in the biggest of moments,” Skubal said. “I think he was great. He did everything he could for his team. He wore it out there sometimes. Chasing box scores and stuff is kind of unfair to judge guys on, because I’m sure he was pitching through some stuff and grinding through some stuff.
“But he had to do it, because he was Clayton Kershaw.”
Dodgers Manager Dave Roberts Points To Major Difference Between Los Angeles And Detroit
According to Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, the difference between Los Angeles and Detroit is clear – the goal for the Dodgers is World Series or bust.
“There’s also a difference between being on a team like the Tigers — and nothing against that organization — where the goal really isn’t to win the World Series. It’s the hope,” Roberts said. “But being here and seeing the standard that we have and it’s like: ‘I’m here to win the World Series. This team has the best chance to win the World Series, and I get to be a part of it.’

item.content:encoded:
Cubs rumors: Chicago insider dumps cold water over any potential Tarik Skubal free agency pursuit appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Chicago Cubs saw their season comes to an end Wednesday night when they were eliminated from the Wild Card round of the National League playoffs by the San Diego Padres. The Cubs lost the series in consecutive games after earning a spot in the postseason in the final days of the season.
While their time in the postseason was short-lived, the Cubs had multiple winning streaks in the early part of the season that allowed them to challenge the Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Central Division. However, the Cubs could not match Milwaukee's consistency throughout the year, and they finished 14 games behind the Brewers.
The Cubs will almost certainly have multiple changes to their roster when the 2027 season gets underway. The Cubs have multiple free agents, including outfielders Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki as well as pitcher Shota Imanaga.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
However, the Cubs are not likely to get involved in the bidding for the top free agent expected to be available. Tarik Skubal of the Dodgers is expected to receive the top contract offer ever made to a pitcher in MLB history.
Skubal was traded by the Detroit Tigers to the Dodgers this summer. Skubal is represented by top player agent Scott Boras, and Skubal is a two-time Cy Young Award winner.
While a number of teams may get involved in the bidding for Skubal, an insider with ties to the Cubs does not believe the team will make a significant bid for the dynamic 29-year-old left-handed pitcher.
The Cubs have already committed about $110 million to future player contracts in 2027.
Related: 1 free agent Cubs must re-sign after losing in postseason to Padres
Related: 3 radical changes Red Sox must make this offseason after humiliating playoff loss

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Tigers Pitcher Acquired for Tarik Skubal Takes Apparent Shot at Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Ricardo Sandoval; Unknown
item.description: It's been two months since the Los Angeles Dodgers shocked the baseball world, trading for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. The Dodgers were always viewed as the frontrunners to trade for the southpaw pitcher; however, it was still hard to believe when it actually happened. item.content:encoded:
It's been two months since the Los Angeles Dodgers shocked the baseball world, trading for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.
The Dodgers were always viewed as the frontrunners to trade for the southpaw pitcher; however, it was still hard to believe when it actually happened.
With the Dodgers' postseason approaching, Skubal is poised to play a vital role in the team's quest for a three-peat. As for Skubal's former team, the Detroit Tigers, they're watching the postseason from home.
The Tigers received what they believed was the best package for Skubal. Detroit acquired outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handed pitchers Brady Smith and River Ryan.
The Dodgers added an ace they hope they can lock up after the 2026 season, and the Tigers retooled their farm system with high-upside talent.
Los Angeles came out as the clear winners in the trade in present times, but Ryan is doing his best to ensure the Tigers come out as the winner when all is said and done.
On top of that, he took a subtle shot at the Dodgers while discussing his transition to the Tigers organization.
“I think the transition, as far as being traded on the injured list and then switching to a whole other organization and continuing through that process, I think Detroit made it really easy," Ryan said in a recent conversation with Just Baseball. "I think it was definitely a lot more hands-on with the Detroit organization. I feel like there was a lot more care involved, which was fantastic."
“They are being really involved in the day-to-day with me,” he added. “They’re all watching my outings, my bullpens. I mean, that’s really it. They’re just really trying to be as involved as they can on a day-to-day basis.”
Ryan also said the transition from Los Angeles to Detroit was pretty easy, since he's been traded before.
“I think since I’ve been through the trading process before, I kind of knew what to expect,” Ryan said. “Transitioning over to another team, meeting all new people, becoming acquainted with everybody. That was pretty easy because I’ve been through it before and I had a reference."
How Did River Ryan’s Dodgers Tenure Unfold?
Ryan was supposed to be a standout pitcher for the Dodgers. Unfortunately for him, his time in Los Angeles was riddled with injuries.
He missed the entire 2025 season recovering from Tommy John surgery and later dealt with minor setbacks like a hamstring issue, prompting the Dodgers to be extremely cautious with his workload.
Ryan, 28, will now do his best to pan out in the big leagues with the Tigers. He made two starts with the Tigers in late-September, alloiwng two runs over 4.1 innings with six strikeouts.

Ricardo Sandoval is a freelance writer with On SI. He is a graduate of California State University, Northridge, and specializes in sports writing, particularly in MLB, NBA and NFL. He previously served as an Associate Editor for Dodgers Nation and has worked with Newsweek and The Sporting News.

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Blue Jays planning to re-explore Japanese market this offseason
item.dc:creator: Vanessa Serrao
item.description: According to Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro, the team plans to re-explore the Japanese market this offseason. On Sept. 8, he became the fifth Japanese-born player to hit 30 home
item.content:encoded:
According to Toronto Blue Jays president and CEO Mark Shapiro, the team plans to re-explore the Japanese market this offseason. The Blue Jays will also be sending a contingency plan to Japan in the offseason, and Shapiro plans to travel there as they look to bolster the lineup.
The Blue Jays have already been successful with recruiting Japanese star Kazuma Okamoto, who had a stellar rookie campaign this season with 33 home runs. On Sept. 8, he became the fifth Japanese-born player to hit 30 home runs, earning a noteworthy milestone achievement.
Signing Okamoto to a four-year, $60 million contract last offseason was a massive win. While the team's offense and power output took a significant step backward this season, Okamoto was the driving force behind the team's power. All things considered, his success has persuaded the team to continue to find more Japanese talent.
While the Blue Jays are targeting Seiya Suzuki from the Chicago Cubs as well, the team has also been eyeing two big Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) stars who are expected to be on the market this winter and have already gained significant attention from MLB teams.
Mark Shapiro says the #BlueJays will send a contingency to Japan this offseason and he may travel there, too, as they look to expand their presence (both baseball and business).
He added that the Japanese market will obviously be something they explore again this winter.
Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato and right-handed pitcher Kaima Taira are two talents that would help enhance the Blue Jays' needs ahead of the 2027 season. Sato would provide the Blue Jays with an elite left-handed power bat who is coming off a dominant 37-home-run season with an explosive 1.012 OPS for the Hanshin Tigers.
With Taira, he is expected to be one of the top arms on the market alongside Tarik Skubal, who is an elite starter and reliever. But as a starter, he led all of NPB with a 1.36 ERA, serving as a commanding presence for the Saitama Seibu Lions.
The Blue Jays would benefit from adding his arm, as he would provide high-upside pitching depth to the rotation as well as a bullpen safety net. His versatility makes him an intriguing option to add as the team faced a heavily taxed pitching staff this season. While the Blue Jays are expected to get Cody Ponce, Bowden Francis and Jose Berrios back in 2027, you can never have enough pitching, and this past season proves it.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have yet to begin their quest for a three-peat during these MLB playoffs, which are already underway, but on paper, LA is going to be a tough out regardless of its opponent.
However, even though the MLB playoffs are underway, it’s not too early to start thinking about the major offseason decision the team faces regarding ace starter Tarik Skubal.
Recently, in an MLB free agent predictions piece, Tarik Skubal is being linked back to the Los Angeles Dodgers on a 10-year deal.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 3 Sudden Roster Moves Amid MLB Playoffs
Dodgers Predicted to Retain Tarik Skubal
Back in August, the Dodgers shocked the MLB world by landing Tarik Skubal in a huge trade with the Detroit Tigers.
However, they (LA) face a big decision regarding his free-agent status, as he is set to hit the open market after the 2026 season.
BleacherReport.com’s Zach Buckley recently predicted LA to retain its new ace via a 10-year deal:
“Prediction: Skubal re-signs with the Dodgers on a 10-year deal.”
“In short, the crystal ball sees this coming down to the Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Mets—two of the biggest spenders in baseball. The Dodgers just made an aggressive move for Skubal at this year’s trade deadline, while the Mets badly need a boost to their rotation. This bidding war should be ferocious, but in the end, the Dodgers’ head start by having Skubal already on the roster could be what pushes them over the edge.”
More MLB on Heavy: MLB World Reacts to Austin Riley Moment in Phillies-Braves Game
Tarik Skubal Has Proved His Worth with Los Angeles
Let’s be clear: the 2X AL Cy Young winner in Tarik Skubal, doesn’t have to prove his worth to anybody, but since joining the Dodgers, he’s made it really hard for the team to ignore that he would be an immense addition to the starting rotation.
Across 10 starts with LA, Skubal holds a 2.61 ERA with 70 strikeouts.
He will be a huge piece to the Dodgers postseason fold, and if he really helps propel LA to a three-peat, that might be enough to truly force Andrew Friedman’s hand in his ongoing contract talks.
Dodgers fans, do you want to bring back Tarik Skubal? And at what price would you be willing to do so?

item.title: [fansided.com] 5 free agent landing spots for Michael King after sterling playoff start
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline

item.content:encoded:
The San Diego Padres blitzed the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card series, 8-0, to put themselves one win away from a date with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. Plenty of Padres deserve credit for Tuesday night's dominant performance, but none more than soon-to-be-free agent Michael King.
San Diego's ace put together one of the best postseason starts in recent memory, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh inning. He finished with seven scoreless frames, allowing one hit, three walks and recording eight strikeouts. As Padres fans celebrate King's masterclass, prospective free agency suitors are chomping at the bit. Here are a few potential landing spots:
Atlanta Braves
The Braves rotation is a bit scarce behind Chris Sale. Tyler Mahle has eviscerated the competition since arriving at the trade deadline, but he's a free agent next winter. AJ Smith-Shawver, J.R. Ritchie and Owen Murphy are all exciting young arms, but it's unclear which of them will click as full-time starters — and how soon. Martín Pérez, one of this season's great surprises for Atlanta, is also an upcoming free agent.
Atlanta doesn't typically pay sticker price on free agent pitchers but there is immense pressure to compete now — right now — in the twilight years of Sale's career. He won't be able to anchor this rotation forever and the Braves need to start hedging their bets, just in case Father Time catches up.
King, with a 3.21 ERA and 1.18 WHIP, has made 32 starts and pitched a career-high 185 innings this season. The Braves need depth and dependability most desperately, and that's something King can provide. It doesn't hurt that he is building a nice postseason résumé for himself.
Baltimore Orioles
Every winter, we all wonder if Baltimore might finally upgrade its pitching staff. The Corbin Burnes era burned bright and fast. Shane Baz was a savvy trade addition last winter, but the Orioles still struggled to field five quality, healthy starters for the 162-game duration of the regular season.
Trevor Rogers, their best pitcher two years running, will now enter free agency. That leaves Baltimore's front office will a clear and immediate need in the rotation. It seems like the O's new ownership group will, on some level, spend more than the previous administration. The Pete Alonso signing was a stark departure from business as usual in Baltimore. As such, it's not hard to envision the O's ponying up for a second-tier ace like Michael King; the Tarik Skubals of the world are still outside their price range, no doubt.
If Kyle Bradish can finally get healthy for a year, and if the O's deign to re-sign Rogers (or pursue another mid-rotation arm in addition to King), this rotation could shape up quite nicely. Baltimore has the offensive firepower to compete in the AL East. King can help round out a postseason-caliber roster.
Toronto Blue Jays
A nightmare Blue Jays season has finally come to an end, but Toronto should be right back in the postseason fray next season with better luck and an productive winter. The Jays front office is probably the most aggressive in baseball outside of L.A. or New York.
Last offseason, their big fish was Dylan Cease, who immediately turned in a Cy Young-caliber campaign. At the trade deadline, Toronto did not strictly sell, despite sitting near the bottom of the standings. The Jays went out and added José Soriano, another frontline starter at the peak of his powers.
Toronto can expect a healtheir Trey Yesavage in 2027, too, so a premium free agent addition (like King) could quickly transform the Blue Jays rotation into one of the deepest and most fearsome in the American League. If Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Toronto's boppers put their best foot forward, there's no reason Toronto can't win the division and compete (again) for a World Series.
Houston Astros
The Astros went bullpen against bullpen in their AL Wild Card series opener against the White Sox. Houston was lucky Chicago only managed six runs, with many, many base-runners stranded in scoring position. That did not mean much for the Astros, unfortunately, as the Chicago bullpen — against all odds — mostly kept a more seasoned Houston lineup in check.
Houston has a proper 1A ace in Hunter Brown, but the rotation behind him is total patchwork. Peter Lambert put together a solid campaign and Ethan Pecko faired well in his first taste of MLB action, but the Astros can't really trust anyone besides Brown. Tatsuya Imai, their prized free agent addition last winter, was little more than a bulk reliever in his rookie season.
The Astros have gotten cheaper and cheaper in recent years and the results are getting worse and worse, predictably. Still, this core has competed for a World Series in the not-so-distant past, and we know ownership is capable of spending at the upper echelon of free agency. King would do a lot to solidify the Astros' pitching plans in 2027.
Chicago Cubs
Injuries decimated the Cubs rotation this season. Justin Steele, Cade Horton and Ben Brown should all return in 2027, which is a major, natural influx of talent. If Edward Cabrera can rebound, the Cubs rotation will be all rainbows and sunshine — at least on paper.
But as this season once again reminded us, what happens "on paper" almost never translates to reality. Shōta Imanaga and Matthew Boyd are both upcoming free agents. Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, Chicago's emergency deadline rentals, are also halfway out the door. There's uncertainty around how exactly the likes of Steele and Horton will perform coming off of major elbow surgeries, too. So the Cubs should play it safe and hyper-focus on pitching depth.
The rotation could be what sends Chicago home against San Diego. So, why not use the Padres own weapons against them in free agency and sign King? "Stability" is a word that comes to mind with King, and that's exactly what the Cubs need right now.

item.title: [themorningsun.com] What went wrong? Tigers boss dissects a disappointing 2026 season
item.dc:creator: Tribune News Service

item.content:encoded:
By Evan Woodbery, mlive.com
DETROIT — Scott Harris didn’t have to spend much time searching for the stretch that doomed the Detroit Tigers’ season.
That miserable May is right there for everyone to see.
The Tigers went 6-22, tumbled into last place in the American League Central and spent the rest of the summer trying to recover. They never really did, finishing 76-86 and missing the postseason for the first time in three years.
Less than 24 hours after the season ended, Harris offered his explanation for how a team that entered the year with championship aspirations wound up 10 games under .500.
“This season, and the fact that we’re sitting here right now, is a missed opportunity for this organization, plain and simple,” the Tigers’ president of baseball operations said Monday at Comerica Park. “We’ve got to get better.”
Some of those explanations are easier to quantify than others. Here’s Harris’ assessment of what went wrong.
The May meltdown
There are a lot of ways to dissect a 162-game season, but the brutal 28-game stretch early in the season was a gut punch to the Tigers’ plans to contend in 2026.
“There are a lot of reasons why we’re sitting here and not in the playoffs right now,” Harris said. “One of them really sticks out above the rest for me. You can’t go 6-22 in a month and expect to punch your ticket to the postseason at this level.”
“I think one of the things that I’m really struggling to process about this year is, in many ways, this roster performed quite well for five months, excluding May.”
Before and after May, the Tigers went 70-64. Even more notably, Harris said, they ranked second in baseball in team ERA, second in wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) and posted a plus-119 run differential.
“That’s playoff-worthy. If anything, our record probably should have been even better than 70-64, given the underlying run production and run prevention.”
Why did May happen?
Harris’ answer began with injuries.
Injuries, and a roster that couldn’t absorb them
The Tigers were hit unusually hard by injuries.
Second baseman Gleyber Torres, outfielder Kerry Carpenter, reliever Will Vest and, of course, ace starter Tarik Skubal missed most or all of the month.
Even without Skubal and Vest, run prevention generally wasn’t the biggest problem. The lineup cratered, with significant at-bats going to fill-ins like Gage Workman and Zack Short. Role players like Jahmai Jones, Zach McKinstry and Matt Vierling were pressed into larger roles while mired in prolonged slumps.
“Our roster never really saw the light of day,” Harris said. “We built a roster that we thought was talented, that many people in this room thought was really talented, and they never all actually got on the field at the same time.”
“It’s really hard to have an honest conversation about this organization in the 2026 season without noting that we put 41 players on the injured list on our 40-man roster this year,” Harris said.
“It’s not an excuse. But at some point, you get to a volume of injuries that becomes destabilizing to your ability to manage a roster. I think it did. It really hurt us in certain sections of this year.”
But Harris also said he didn’t build enough depth beyond the active roster to handle what happened.
“Upon reflection, our inability to overcome adversity in real time starts with me,” Harris said. “I didn’t build enough depth into this roster this year. The vulnerabilities in this roster got exposed in May, and it cost us.”
Harris said Detroit entered the season knowing it would become deeper as the summer progressed, with prospects like center fielder Max Clark slated to arrive later.
“I think the main mistake that I made was our depth was coming a little bit too late, basically in all facets of our roster,” Harris said.
The Tigers were also reluctant to add players who might eventually block those prospects. That left them trying short-term fixes like Short and, later, outfielder James Outman.
“We didn’t want to block young players,” Harris said. “We didn’t want to trade for depth players that were ultimately going to box Max out of the big leagues. So we were trying to thread that needle, and I think it probably was a mistake in the end.
“We probably should have just strengthened our depth and made sure that we could get through April and May intact.”
Harris said Detroit was particularly thin with up-the-middle defenders, back-end relievers and starting-pitching depth.
“We couldn’t really afford to lose back-end relievers,” he said. “We couldn’t really afford to lose starting depth. And we couldn’t really afford to have our pinch hitters’ performance sag in leverage spots.”
All that happened in May.
“Could we afford to have all (of that) happen at the same time? No, clearly not,” Harris said. “We went 6-22 that month, and so I feel very responsible for that.”
Too much mixing and matching
The Tigers have built much of their identity by playing the matchups, mixing and matching and asking players to be versatile.
But Harris suggested for the first time that they may have become too reliant on it.
When role players do well, like Andy Ibáñez in 2024 and Jahmai Jones in 2025, it’s a huge boost in high-leverage moments.
But when players in those roles struggle, as they did during key points in 2026, it can be devastating.
Harris sees the arrival of more players like Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark, who the Tigers believe can contribute both offensively and defensively and play nine innings every day, as a way to reduce that dependence.
“I think we’re probably going to start playing differently a little bit,” Harris said. “We’re going to be less reliant on pinch-hit appearances. We’re going to be less reliant on the mixing and matching because we have more two-way players growing through the system that can help us both defensively and offensively.”
Lagging in leverage
Based on their run differential, the Tigers had an expected record of 89-73, not 76-86.
Of course, baseball doesn’t work that way. But the gap between what actually happened and what their run differential suggests should have happened is one of the most perplexing storylines of 2026.
“When you take a look at our season, our run differential says one thing and our record says something very different,” Harris said.
“If we had played up to our run differential, we probably would have won the division again.”
“That doesn’t matter,” he added. “I can’t stand up here and just cite different metrics and tell you this is what we should have done and act like we did it. We didn’t do it.”
“So the question that I’m going to ask myself is: How do we play in a way that either meets or exceeds our run production and run prevention performance, our underlying performance?”
It’s no secret the Tigers won a lot of blowouts and lost a ton of close games. They went an astonishing 23-52 in games decided by two runs or fewer.
That’s largely because the Tigers performed better in low- and medium-leverage situations than they did when the leverage spiked.
The numbers were particularly stark among relievers.
Tigers relievers faced 370 batters in high-leverage situations and posted a jaw-dropping 9.21 ERA (5.62 FIP). Opponents posted an .855 OPS against them and hit a league-high 19 home runs in those situations. A staggering 21.8 percent of opposing fly balls landed in the seats. No other team was even close in that category.
Maybe that’s bad luck. But it’s also bad news for any team trying to contend.
“We really struggled in high leverage,” Harris said. “We’ve got to get to the bottom of that. We’ve got to figure out why that happens.”
Harris said sometimes the problem was that the game never should have reached a high-leverage situation in the first place.
“We’ve got to do a better job of staying out of those high-leverage situations,” Harris said.
That means looking beyond the final pitch of a loss.
“There were a number of games that we saw this year where we got walked off or our bullpen blew a late lead that I don’t think you can actually put on our bullpen,” Harris said.
“Some of them you can, for sure. But some of them you can’t.
“Some of them you can actually look deeper into the game and you could find the core issue, which was we didn’t create separation before, or we made a misplay in the third inning and coughed up one or two runs, or we made a baserunning mistake in the fifth inning,” Harris said.
“We let our opponent stay in the game, create this one- and two-run game, and then we ultimately lost it.”
Harris believes the changing makeup of the roster can help with that.
The Tigers are getting younger, faster and, in Harris’ view, more athletic. He expects that to mean better defense, more aggressive baserunning and more ways to create separation without simply waiting for a home run.
“We’re going to take the extra base. We’re also going to steal bases. And we’re also going to put a lot more pressure, and that’s all going to contribute to creating separation when we’re not hitting,” Harris said.
“We’re still going to hit, but we’re also going to be able to flex different muscles at different times that can help us stay out of those high-leverage situations.”
Harris said the Tigers are already conducting what he called a “pre-mortem” on the 2027 roster, trying to anticipate next year’s vulnerabilities before they arise.
“What if this happens? What are we going to do? What if this happens? What are we going to do?” Harris said.
That includes underperformance as well as injuries.
“If a guy gets out of the gate really slow, what are we going to do?” Harris said. “Those are the questions we have to ask ourselves.
“When I talk about learning lessons from the season, that’s one of the lessons that I’ve learned.”

item.title: [si.com] The Potentially Fatal Flaw For Each MLB Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Ryan Phillips
item.description: The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early. item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] NY Mets Rumor Reveals Top Offseason Priority: Will It Be Tarik Skubal?
item.dc:creator: Jason Burgos
item.description: New York Mets fans hoping that the team makes Tarik Skubal their top offseason priority received some bad news in a new rumor. item.content:encoded:
New York Mets fans hoping that the team makes Tarik Skubal their top offseason priority received some bad news in a new rumor.
On Sunday, a very disappointing season for the Mets came to a close with a 6-4 loss to the Washington Nationals. The team with the second-highest payroll in MLB entered the offseason with World Series hopes and instead finished last in the National League East with a 74-88 record.
After addressing who will be their full-time manager — they signed interim skipper Andy Green to a three-year deal last week — and adding more talented minds to the front office, the club will now shift to improving the roster for 2027.
President David Stearns revealed that the starting staff will be the part of the roster the front office focuses on improving. That is why making a strong push to sign the two-time Cy Young winner would make sense. The combo of NL Rookie of the Year candidate Nolan McLean and Skubal could be a dynamite duo for many years.
However, according to The Athletic's Will Sammon, the Mets will go bargain shopping to add pitchers for a specific reason.
"League sources said the club is expected to aggressively pursue options at the lower end of the starting pitcher market for better depth. For two straight years, Stearns and his front office failed to cushion the rotation with enough viable alternatives in case of injury or poor performance. In 2025, Griffin Canning's injury was too big of a burden. In May, the Mets failed to overcome Clay Holmes' fibula injury in time to save their season. It simply can't happen again."
The strategy makes sense. And Sammon notes that good starting pitching depth has played a role in the consistent success of teams like the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays. However, for fans hoping the team makes big moves to improve the rotation this summer, more discount shopping by Stearns will further frustrate them.
